speechtext:
["I wish for only two or three minutes to voice my opposition to this bill. It is the very same bill in a new form as was proposed before, giving vast powers to the governor in council. As hon. members know, under the original War Measures Act and bill No. 15 the courts of this countrythe high courts, the county courts, and the magistrates' courts-have before them cases to decide and give decisions based on the powers herein of the governor in council.
After the dominion-provincial conference which met last week some of those persons who spoke to the newspapers described bill No. 15 as the Donald Gordon plan. This new plan gives the governor in council powers to look after the maintenance of the armed forces of Canada, all trade and commerce and so on. In fact, it is the identical style of bill with the identical powers.
They have abolished these controls in Australia, and the President of the United States has practically eliminated them in that great country. Let me point out that under section 2 there is no doubt that people will be summonsed to court-police courts and other courts of competent jurisdiction-to answer to the same irksome control offences. Is this Liberalism as we have it in this country to-day? Is this what you call Liberalism? -control over the lives of every person, control over every man, woman and child in Canada, and the abolition of statutes which for 200 years have protected the liberty of the subject and of all reference to the law courts who have no control? Everything in the bill is removed from the controls of those courts. They would not stand for this in the United States. Why, we have a regular small standing army of officials in that country. The government knows something of what is going on. That standing army would reach from here to Lansdowne park. The expeditionary force we have over there should learn something of what is being done in that country to abolish all controls. But they have learned nothing.
Over there they have abolished controls. Under section 2 of this bill the small and large businessman would be put out of business. The difference between the new bill and the old one is the difference between Tweedledum and Tweedledee. That is the only difference between these two plans.
Under paragraph (a) the governor in council has power to provide for and maintain the armed forces of Canada during the occupation of enemy territory; it has power to facilitate the readjustment of industry, and also other powers. Small and large business, and every manufacturer in the country have been asking for the removal of these irksome controls. How does the government expect war-time economies to be turned into peace-time economies of large and small business when we have these irksome controls placed upon individuals?
Questions", 'The people whom we have been giving credit < for the formulation of this new plan will be glad to be free of it, when they see how unpopular it is throughout the country. I know something of the way in which these irksome controls have operated during the war years and the effect they have had on business generally.
Section stands.
Progress reported.']

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO POLICY OF UNITED KINGDOM GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement in answer to a recent question by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Eraser).
The question of the hon. member touches on a matter that has been of great concern to this government for some time and has been the subject of repeated consultation with United Kingdom representatives both here and in London. The situation with which we are now faced is one which was foreseen and one which both governments have hoped to avoid. Unfortunately, that has not been possible. It was anticipated that these questions would arise after the termination of mutual aid and lend lease and, accordingly, plans were laid for discussions with the United Kingdom to follow immediately on the conclusion of the United Kingdom-United States talks which we expected to be finished early in November.
The Washington discussions have continued much longer than was anticipated, and of necessity our talks with the United Kingdom have not yet taken place. Because of the magnitude of the problems involved, it would have been quite impossible for us to have any productive discussions with the United Kingdom until the results of the United States talks were known.
On the matter of the import policy which the United Kingdom is pursuing, I am now able to give the house a statement that we have received from the United Kingdom government:
The stringency of Britain's external financial position resulting from the war, has left the United Kingdom government with no alternative but to restrict by licence for the time being, the United Kingdom's imports of manufactured
goods. Until her industry can be reestablished, and her export trade developed to a level substantially in excess of pre-war, the United Kingdom will have an adverse balance in her overseas payments. This means that she must forgo, for the present, many articles which she would like to import. Thus, essential supplies of foodstuffs and raw materials have, for the present, to receive priority, and in the case of manufactured goods, import licences have perforce to be restricted to such goods as are urgently needed to supplement home production and quicken her economic recovery.
This, however, is an interim policy only, dictated by present necessities. As Britain's external financial position improves, there should follow a progressive relaxation in import controls. It is the aim of the United Kingdom government that this relaxation should be as rapid as possible, but it is difficult to make any forecast as to the rate of relaxation since this will depend on many factors, particularly the extent of such financial assistance as may be forthcoming from abroad, the improvement in United Kingdom exports, and the reduction in the United Kingdom's expenditure on external commitments consequent on the war. The United Kingdom government hope, however, that it may be possible to proceed to a more definite policy before very long.
In the meantime, certain Canadian firms have approached the United Kingdom government for facilities to establish production in the United Kingdom. I am informed, however, that it is not the policy of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom to use the import licensing system to bring pressure on Canadian firms to do so.
This is the end of the statement by the British authorities. I wish briefly to supplement this statement. It is gratifying to make public . this assurance that the policy which the United Kingdom finds itself forced to adopt is an interim policy only and is subject to reconsideration in the light of changing circumstances. It is our hope that the conclusion of the Washington negotiations is not far distant, and I can assure the house that - immediately the results of those discussions are known, we shall proceed to examine these with United Kingdom representatives and discuss with them arrangements for formal discussions between the two governments which we would hope to hold shortly.
Apart altogether from the statement by the United Kingdom which I have just read, I should like very briefly to draw the attention of the house to a matter which may serve to illustrate the reluctance of British authorities to discriminate against imports from Canada and of their desire to safeguard our traditional place in the British market, in so far as present circumstances permit.
The house is aware that we have been in consultation with the British authorities on a number of important individual cases. The British austerity programme has dictated the continuation of the general policy of a four-page newspaper. But as the result of Cana-
Prince Rupert Dry Dock

dian representations that have been made, assurances have now been received from the United Kingdom that Canada will supply a fair part of the reduced British consumption of newsprint.
Other representations made resulted in the reinstatement of orders for agricultural implements which the United Kingdom authorities had cancelled some months ago. The Canadian export board of my department estimated that these cancellations alone would have amounted to more than 31,600,000. Continuing representations are being made on other matters, and I cite two cases simply to illustrate the general British attitude and their desire to cooperate as much as their circumstances permit in acceding to our representations.
Personally I do not in any way question the assurances that are given from time to time by leaders of the United Kingdom government with respect to the principles that will guide the future trading policies of Great Britain. I recognize, however, that the time which may elapse in giving them full effect is a matter of the utmost concern to individual Canadian companies that have relied heavily upon the British market, and to our own national trading position in the great British market.
I need hardly add that I realize that it is of importance that we press on as quickly as possible with our discussions with the United Kingdom authorities, having in mind that we must reach the earliest possible solution of our United Kingdom-Canada trade arrangements which are so vital to our whole trading position.

position of employment. -I am informed by the Canadian National that 622 shipyard workers were in employment at Prince Rupert on November 24. This staff will be reduced around the end of January to between 400 and 450, when the first vessel will be completed, and will be further reduced to about 250 by the end of February, when the second vessel is expected to be completed. Normal pre-war employment at Prince Rupert has been between 90 and 100. speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, December 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of bill No. 15, to confer certain powers upon the governor in council during the national emergency following the war.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I had just concluded a few general remarks on the stand we take with respect to this bill, and was about to consider the principle of the bill itself. I realize that there' is a duty on all members to be as brief as possible ip. these discussions, and I should like to assure you, sir, and through you all hon. members, that I shall endeavour to carry out that duty. In order to make my case coherent, however, I should like merely to outline again the stand which we take, and then develop our case against the principle of this bill.
First, we are very much concerned with the constitutional safeguards which protect the rights and freedom of parliament and the rights and freedom of the individual. We are particularly concerned with the supremacy of parliament in the legislative sphere.
Second, this bill-and indeed any measure which seeks for whatever reason to take away those safeguards and give to the executive powers and privileges which rightly belong to parliament and are assured to parliament by the constitution-is, on the face of it, a bad measure. If it'infringes the constitution it should be resisted. However, it must be admitted, and it has been admitted by us without reservation, that in an emergency situation there is justification for a greater or lesser departure from the strict rules of constitutionality. In this particular case it is the contention of the government that in order to maintain the economic structure of the country and to secure an orderly transition from war-time to peace-time economy, emergency powers are necessary. We are therefore prepared to make certain concessions; but in view of what I have said with regard to the way we feel about the supremacy of parliament and the sanctity of the constitution, we are not prepared to make, further concessions than are absolutely necessaiy to accomplish the objects the government has in mind.
When we saw bill No. 15 as it was originally printed and distributed, the second reading of which is now before the house, we considered it wholly bad, inasmuch as it asked not for the delegation of powers, but for a complete abdication, a complete denial of

constitutional principles. The situation has been confused by the circulation of the new bill 15. With the permission of the house I should like to refer briefly to that bill. I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) will permit me to congratulate him on some aspects of the new bill, inasmuch as it does show a certain willingness to concede, and for that we are extremely grateful. But the bill still goes a great deal too far; therefore, in view of the way we feel about the constitution, the bill is still bad. We are encouraged, if I may put it that way, by the generosity of the Minister of Justice in maknig the concessions which he has made, and knowing that the Minister of Justice listens to representations made when the subject matter under discussion is the constitutional right and the rights and liberties of. the individual, I feel encouraged to discuss the bill. I should like the minister to make further concessions, and . those concessions can be indicated in the discussion of the general principle of the bill.
Our objection to the bill as it stands is that the powers sought by the government are still far too wide. They are so wide as to constitute an unwarranted attack on the constitution, and to involve an unjustifiable violation of the principles of the liberty of the subject; therefore we are unable to accept the principle of the bill.
The main basis on which we say this bill is still too wide is to be found in clause 4, which reads as follows:
The orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act or pursuant to authority created under the said act in force immediately before the day this act comes into force shall, while this act is in force, continue in force and effect. . .
It has been conceded by government speakers, and was conceded last night, that many of ,the regulations and things done under the War Measures Act were,'strictly speaking, un-[DOT] constitutional. It was conceded that although justifiable in time of war, they were not justifiable in time of peace. It was further conceded that it is desirable to curtail these powers on the part of the executive and to discontinue them as soon as possible. The strongest possbile case for that position was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his speech last night.
In both the original bill 15 now before the house and the new bill 15 which has been circulated with proposed amendments we find that it is desired to continue in force all those acts and things done under the War Measures Act. The effect of section 4 of the new bill, which is section 5 of the old bill, is that we are asked to give, sight unseen, assent to a number of measures the content and effects of

National Emergency
which are unknown to us. I submit to the minister that it is not fair to ask this house, it is not fair to ask any members of this house, so to endorse provisions, the content of which we do not know and the effects of which we do not know. It is not necessary; therefore, it is bad. As it is such a vital and integral part of this bill, it constitutes a valid ground for objection to the principle of the bill.
I have said,' Mr. Speaker, that it is not necessary to seek this blanket endorsement for all that was done under the War Measures Act. In substantiation of that statement I should like to refer briefly to the bill recently introduced in the British house, the Supplies and Services (Transitional Powers) bill. In the first place this confers no new power on [DOT]the government to make regulations, as does bill 15 in this house. In the view of the British government they have sufficient power already under the defence regulations to do everything required during the transitional period from war to peace. They do regard it as necessary to continue certain of those powers; but instead of asking for a blanket continuation the British government has adopted the proper constitutional method and defined the four categories of powers which they require for the maintenance and the orderly regulation of the economy of their country. They have defined those powers and then have said, "The only regulations we are going to ask this house to continue are the specific regulations falling within these four categories." Here is the relevant portion of the British act, which is found in section 1:
If it appears to His Majesty to he necessary or expedient that any defence regulation to which this section applies should have effect for the purpose of so maintaining, controlling [DOT]and regulating supplies and services. . .
Then they define the four categories within which those regulations may fall, giving the four heads under which they need power, and go on to say:
.... he may by order in council direct that the regulation shall have effect by virtue of this act. . .
In other words the regulations already existing must deal with one or other of the four subjects; in the second place the regulations must have specific consideration and extension, and in the third place the regulations will be reviewed and adapted to meet the needs of the moment. In elaboration of this I should like to read some extracts from the British Hansard for Tuesday, October 9, 1945. On that date the home secretary, Mr. Ede, brought into the British house this bill to which I have referred. In moving second reading he said, at page 111:
I want to make it quite clear at the outset that the government intend to retain only those war-time powers which are desirable in the public interest.
Then at page 115, referring to the orders made under the British Defence Regulations Acts, he said:
Those acts will now expire on the 24th February next. We have decided that we will not ask the house to continue them beyond that date.
In the first place only those powers necessary were being sought. In the second place none of the others would be asked to be continued beyond that date. Then at page 119 he went on to say:
. . . except for a limited period in respect of
?riee control, the bill confers no power to make resh regulations for the purpose of the transition period, but only a power to make any of the existing defence regulations contained in parts III and IV of the defence (general) regulations . . . applicable to the new purposes of the reconstruction period . . .
And further down on that page:
The existing regulations which will be continued will have to be justified to the house.
And finally.
These orders in council, bringing the defence, regulations into the scope of this bill will have to be laid before both houses and will be subject to annulment by resolution of either house.
There, I submit, is the proper constitutional method to follow: first, to define the categories of the powers you require; second, to say that only those existing regulations which fall within those categories will be continued; third, that even those you seek to continue will be brought into this house and the need for them and their relevancy to this act explained, and then they will be continued in force under this act; finally, that all these regulations, even those we continue, should be subject to annulment by resolution of either house, not as in this act by this house alone. That, I submit,' is the proper course and is all that is required to give the government sufficient power. It is the course which should be followed here.
In the preamble of the new bill it seems that this is the intention of the government. At line 21 of the preamble I find these words:
. . . and whereas in the existing circumstances [DOT]it is essential that certain acts and things done and authorized and certain orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act be continued in force . . .
1 That would seem to imply that only certain specific regulations and orders were asked to be continued; but, as I have pointed out, that is not the effect of section 4 of the bill.
National Emergency

Therefore I would ask the minister to see to it that the implications contained in the preamble of this bill, and the provision contained in the British bill, are actually incorporated in the bill now before the house. The principle of the bill would then be far more acceptable to all hon. members, and, I am sure, - also to all the people of the country, because they would know what regulations would affect them. It is a well-known principle that ignorance of the law is no excuse for any offence which may be committed, but I defy anyone to know what is the law when that law is contained in ninety or a hundred thousand orders in council and regulations. I think that is one of the strongest possible cases that could be made to require the government to tell us w-hat laws, what powers, what orders in council are being continued by virtue of this present bill.

speechtext:
If that is the case I can only say that this statement is most inconsistent with the statement of the then acting Prime Minister (Mr. Usley) that it was not in accordance with government policy to table the orders in council passed since September 6 of this year. I am trying to present a case to the minister, and so far I have tried to avoid appearing unduly critical. I must say, however, that suspicions are aroused. We should like to regard this bill in the best possible light; we should like to believe in the intentions of the minister and of the government, but suspicions are aroused when we are denied access to the information we seek as to what has been done by order in

council, and in the second place when we are asked to approve, sight unseen, everything that has been done.
I am content to leave my case there, because I think it cannot fail to commend itself to the Minister of Justice. A great deal of work may be involved, but surely it is worth that to see to it that the people of this country know what are the laws which bind them.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our particular objection to the bill as it now stands. I should like to conclude by making a few remarks on the general principles governing the whole situation, which I feel must be said before this measure can be allowed to pass. What I shall present now is the larger application of the particular remarks I have just made.
We oppose this bill on a question of principle, in the belief that it is an excessive infringement of constitutional rights. We oppose it because it goes farther than it, has any right to go. Liberty is perhaps-no, I will say liberty is certainly-the most precious possession of our heritage, the greatest privilege guaranteed to us by our constitution; and therefore the features of the constitution which guarantee it are most vigorously to be fought for. No features of our constitution are so surely protective of liberty as the freedom and supremacy of parliament and the right of the subject to the protection of the established law of the land. In the pursuit of liberty we have just concluded a war; we should be willing to spare no effort to secure and maintain liberty now in Canada. Therefore we say: Let no man, let. no government dare lightly to ask us to agree to a surrender or even to an infringement of either of these two rights given us by the constitution. While we are ready to agree to the handing over of powers and the denial for the moment, of the rule of law and. the supremacy of democratic processes, in order to attain certain specific ends, and within certain specific limitations, we are justified nevertheless, in taking the strongest possible issue with the demand, such as we find here, for the wholesale and abject surrender of these rights.
As hon. members know, many of the powers vested in the governor in council-and these are legislative powers we are dealing with- powers the property of parliament, not executive powers properly vested in the cabinet- are, when embodied in orders in council, given such form as to limit in a most drastic manner the liberty of the subject. T have in mind such things as taking away from a subject the right of resort to the courts, denying a person the right of appeal from the acts of the controllers, and provisions that where investigations are being made into the con-

National Emergency
duet of Canadian citizens under certain regulations, such citizens shall be deprived of their right to counsel, deprived of their protection under the criminal code, and then made liable to prosecution as a result of anything they may say during that investigation.
It is realized that in war the delegation of powers to controllers is necessary. The delegation of powers to make regulations is also necessary. But as I have indicated, this system, when carried out, is full of dangers to the liberty of the individual. That is why we object to any delegation of legislative powers which is not Essential.
In support of what I have said I would read from the report of the committee on ministers' powers appointed by Lord Chancellor Sankey in Great Britain in 1932. Dealing with the new principle of delegating legislative authority, the eomniittee made certain observations which I now quote with approval. I would refer first to page 5 of this report, which states:
Between liberty and government there is an age-long conflict. It is of vital importance that the new policy,-
That is, the policy of legislation by delegated authority-
-while truly promoting liberty by securing better conditions of life for the people of this country, should not, in its zeal for interference, deprive them of their initiative and independence which are the nation's most valuable assets.
And again at page 6:
It cannot, we think, be denied .that prima facie this involves an infringement of that rule of law which is "a characteristic of the English constitution." In this context we may quote a statement of the ideal of justice which should always be an aim of British statesmanship:
"Amid the cross-currents and shifting sands of public life the law is like a great rock upon which a man may set his feet and be safe, while the inevitable inequalities of private life are not so dangerous in a country where every citizen knows that in the law courts, at any rate, he can get justice."

It is a principle in our constitution, one which has remained inviolate from at least the seventeenth century and which has been the envy of all those who at various times have suffered from tyranny, that no man should be denied the right of access to the courts, and further that the judiciary must be independent of the executive. Thus liberty of the individual is assured. And when we find, as we have found in investigating many of these orders in council, not that they take issue with the courts or try to dictate to them, but that they tell the subject that he shall have no right of appeal to the courts, then I say an attack is being made upon the very foundations of our liberty. It is because that sort of thing has been done, under the War Measures Act, because it is sought to carry over into this measure all the things that have been done under the War Measures Act, and because we see in this measure no suggestion of safeguard for the principles and rights of which I have spoken, that we are justified in opposing the principle of the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received several letters expressing strong disapproval of this bill. I will quote only the objections made by the League of Montreal Property Owners:
Dear Sir,
Since October 11, 1941, the League of Montreal Property Owners has informed you of its grievances against the rent control set-up and suggested means of improving the sad lot of its members.
Bill 15, as amended, is now before^ the house. We earnestly beg that a clause be inserted in the bill providing that property owners be restored the rights to which they are entitled and which were suspended during the war, in order that their property may afford them more profitable earnings.
Hoping, dear sir, that you will give this request, your best attention, please believe me, Yours very truly,
(Signed) Arthur Lussier, Secretary.
This letter speaks for itself. There is no need for me to comment upon it since its request is based on a most elementary principle of justice.
National Emergency

Is the bill now before the house necessary, is it even advisable? Under the National Resources Mobilization Act which affects both manpower and materials, all power is vested in the government, and the latter has availed itself, in fact still avails itself fully of its authority. It is free to extend or curtail controls or restrictions in due course, as is evidenced by the following extract taken from page 148 of the 1945 Recapitulation Issue of Canada at War:
Since the end of the war in Europe some restrictions on the production of civilian goods have been removed altogether. The Department of Munitions and 'Supply and the Wartime Prices and Trade Board have both announced a policy of gradual relaxation of the controls as soon as the supply situation justifies.
A state of war still exists in Canada. Here is a quotation taken from page 2 of the 1945 Recapitulation Issue of Canada at War:
. . by and with the advice of Our Privy-Council for Canada . . .
Now Therefore We do hereby Declare and Proclaim that a State of War with the German Reich exists and has existed in Our Dominion of -Canada as and from the tenth day of September, 1939."
I am not aware that the National Resources Mobilization Act, affecting both manpower and materials, has been repealed. Therefore, I find this bill altogether useless. Are more extensive powers sought? That would be detrimental to the prerogatives and privileges of the provinces that have already been bled white.
Here is a further extract taken from page 135 of Canada at War:
The planning -and execution of the federal government's war-time programme of income taxation h-as been greatly facilitated by the withdrawal of the provincial governments from the fields of personal and corporation income taxes for the period of the w,ar. This withdrawal was effected in 1941 by formal agreement between the federal and each provincial government. The provinces have been compensated for the -loss suffered by repealing their own taxes.
Did the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) wish to imply in the house a couple of days ago that the provinces would agree to the clauses and conventions set out in the bill? If such is the case, I advise the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) without further ado, that I am willing to accept the clauses of the bill now before the house; otherwise, however, I would have to oppose the measure in the interest of the respective provincial prerogatives and jurisdictions.
At the close of hostilities the government's first duty should be to recognize the efforts made by the Canadians by restoring the prerogatives of parliament. The time has come
to abolish the restrictions and controls which paralyze agricultural, commercial and industrial development. Otherwise the process of reestablishing the members of our arm-ed forces in civil life will be an exceedingly slow one. Canadians who have fought valiantly in this war expect the party in power to give them new directions which will enable them to take an active part in restoring Canada's economic life. Young people, whose career has been interrupted by the war, are entitled more than\ anyone else to employment and social welfare. We should find an immediate solution to the problem of employment in civil industries. The people are demanding, that production of several essential articles be resumed. Sometimes there are delays which the people are at a loss to explain in view of the abundance of raw materials and labour in this country. We have no right to refuse for the achievement of peace similar sacrifices to those made for the prosecution of the war. The reestablishment of soldiers in civil life must be carried out with diligence and method. Do you think it is fair that in a country like ours veterans who are returning to Canada should find themselves without a dwelling? What good is it to a soldier to be a Canadian and to have sacrificed everything for his country if he cannot even find a place to live?
For years, boards which are not responsible to the people have been daily encroaching on the privileges and on the mandate of duly elected members of parliament. Now that the .war has come to an end those boards should be abolished and parliament's supremacy restored. Those wartime boards have already lasted long enough. We must abolish those states within the state and reestablish responsible government. Canada has sacrificed everything so that liberty and democracy may triumph. The existence of wartime boards which are not responsible to the people of Canada is a challenge to liberty and democracy. For everybody's sake it is time that this dictatorship be eradicated.
In a recent speech in the . British House of Commons, former Prime Minister Churchill stated as follows:
Whatever may be our views on socialism and free entarprise it would be in the general interest that we set in motion the large, -as well as the small wheels of 'life and industry. And fo-r this we need men.
In attacking the Labour government's demobilization plan as inadequate, he stated that it was "the source of our national difficulties".
And he added:
While we are keeping men and women in the armed forces without sufficient reason, there can be no speedy reestablishment.

National Emergency
Thousands of Canadians are not alone in demanding demobilization and the abolition of those boards which are not accountable to the people. Former Prime Minister Churchill rightly claims that failure to do so is the chief cause of the difficulties experienced by his country. He has been urging the British government to demobilize men and women in larger number in order that they may help restore production in all fields. Who can question the experience and the sincerity of the former prime minister? Like England, Canada feels the scarcity of goods. The time has come to promote civilian industry. Let us give back to industry, trade and agriculture the help which they require.
Finally, the abolition of controls, the repeal of the mobilization and conscription act and the granting of an amnesty to defaulters and deserters would enable our young men to devote their energies to the economic reconstruction of Canada. Useful jobs are awaiting them. Why deprive the country- of the contribution which they are in a position to make through their initiative and their efforts?
In support of my contentions, I quote these further statements by Winston Churchil, which appeared in La Presse of Montreal on October 22, 1945:
The regrettable shortage of goods will continue. The government cannot allow the people to spend their savings lest an undue increase in prices take place. Shortages will be invoked ito justify the continuation of controls and the latter will prolong the scarcity of goods.
He asked the government to release the men from the services and to "set in motion the machinery of economic life". He stated that he would be ashamed to bear the responsibility of the government's statement on demobilization.
The moment has come to bring back to the country the men who have conquered, he stated, and no acute unemployment is to be feared. All industries require workers and there are numerous useful and fruitful tasks to be accomplished.
Since Mr. Churchill urges the return to England of British soldiers and their demobilization, are we not entitled to urge the repatriation to Canada of thousands of our soldiers and the demobilization of our men who are occupying Germany and the conquered countries? Has Canada not played her part in the achievement of victory? To paraphrase a sentence made famous by the former British prime minister who said: "Give us the tools and we will finish the job", I say to the government: Give our youth the tools necessary to achieve and win the peace.
'Let us make no mistake about it, peace exists in appearance only.	-

The hon. member for Matapedia-Matane is misinterpreting my statement. I fail to see by what right he distorts the arguments I am developing in this house. However, his question does not deserve any answer. I simply quote the statements of the former prime minister of England and apply them to Canadian politics as anyone might do in similar circumstances. I will therefore ask my hon. friend to feel no anxiety on this score.
I was saying that peace is only apparent at the present time. Europe is, to a certain extent, dominated by communism. A system which is worse than the dictatorship crushed by the united nations rules over the liberated countries in the name of justice, Christianity and right. The Atlantic charter, the Yalta resolutions, the war objectives of the allies are trampled under foot. Soviet Russia is causing its whole weight to bear on nations which it is its mission to revive and not to overrun. Religious authorities of Lithuania and the Slavic states have protested against such brutal treatment.
Let us beware lest, under cover of the critical times which Canada will experience, subversive elements might spread through the land. Having won the war would be of no avail were we to lose the peace. True peace is not attainable through the violation of other peoples' rights. The respective jurisdictions of the provincial and federal authorities are clearly defined. Under war-time measures, provincial rights have been encroached upon time and again when they have not been positively ignored. What was unwarranted in time of war is unjustifiable in time of peace. Why attempt to delay the proclamation of peace for the sole purpose of maintaining a bureaucratic, system which has replaced the elected representatives of the people? The time has come to return to normal living and do away with restrictions, boards and controls.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government is endowed with all the powers to that end, but I repeat what I said a few moments ago. If the provincial premiers, at the recent federal-provincial conference, have approved the clauses and conventions contained in the present bill, I am willing to uphold them, otherwise, I shall oppose them.

Mr. Speaker, as the leader of this group stated a week ago Friday, we did not think that the government should seek such blanket and absolute powers as those put forth in sections 3 and 5 of the bill. We therefore stated that when the bill reached the committee stage we would move certain amendments. However, the government now intends to move a new bill as an amendment in committee stage. This new bill apparently has come into being largely as a result of the conference which took place between the federal government and the provincial premiers, and also no doubt as a result of consideration of the various criticisms which were made in this houje when the bill was first introduced.
The new bill is certainly an improvement on the old one, but the powers of control are still very wide. I think we all agree, however, that certain controls are essential at this time and will continue to be essential for several months; and therefore it is concerning these controls which are essential that I wish to say a few words at this time.
I think people across Canada from one end to the other are looking forward to the daj' when these controls will be just an unpleasant memory. They are fed up with being at the mercy of the whims and the tyrannies of a bunch of bureaucrats. It is a strange thing that when you give some people a little bit of power it seems to have about the same effect on them as when you give some people a drink of liquor; it goes to their heads, and. from being just ordinary likeable individuals they become a great big nuisance, a headache to themselves and everybody concerned.
On the other hand, while recognizing the needs for these controls in war time, the people are demanding that they be eliminated at the earliest possible day. Obviously controls cannot cease upon the day of victory. Conditions arising from war will continue for many weeks and months after the war, and until those conditions have been removed, controls will have to continue, unless of course we are prepared to face consequences which might very well be chaotic. If that comes about, I would say, it will not be the wealthy people of the country who will suffer but the people in the lower income brackets, and especially veterans and their dependents who will be trying to start life anew. They would be the main sufferers from any chaotic state of affairs that might ensue such as existed at the conclusion of the war 1914-18.
In addition to price controls certain controls are needed in connection with transport-

ation in order to expedite the repatriation of the troops from overseas; and m,any of the benefits and preferences awarded to the veterans to-day having been passed under orders in council adopted by virtue of the War Measures Act, should the War Measures Act cease, those benefits would largely go out of existence.
Practically all war-time conditions requiring controls arise from a shortage of consumer goods and services. It is well to remember that during the war approximately fifty per cent of the production went for war purposes, and in spite of very heavy taxation during the war, billions of dollars of savings were accumulated in the form of bonds, war saving certificates and refundable taxes, so that these savings would become a very active demand for the class of goods' which the people were not able to obtain during the war and which are still in short supply. Therefore until we complete the '[DOT]reconversion of industry from a war-time to a peace-time footing, it will be necessary to curtail the demand for that type of goods.
We have also of course a heavy responsibility in regard to the devastated areas of Europe and other parts of the world as a consequence of the war. Unless we want to witness wholesale starvation in those areas we, along with other nations that have not been devastated as a result of the war, will have to make large contributions to those areas; and that of course is bound to reduce the amount of goods available for distribution in this country.
Again, certain imports have been scarce during the war owing to lack of shipping and to the fact that the countries from which we obtained those imports in the past were overrun by the enemy. I point this out to show that the answer to all these questions is the expansion in production of consumer goods and services. Therefore the question which the government must ask themselves is whether their policy is one that will bring about the most rapid expansion of production, thereby making it possible to eliminate these controls in the shortest possible time. For instance, what assurance is being given industry to-day that not only will there be an immediate demand, but a continuing demand, for their total output? What assurance is being given industry to-day that when the accumulation of savings, causing a demand for goods, has been spent, other demands will take their place? And again, what assurance is being given industry that when the devastated areas have been rehabilitated, when they have rebuilt their industries and are once more in a position to export their goods in payment for imports,

National Emergency
we shall be willing to accept those goods without the danger of their flooding the market and causing unemployment in this country?
That assurance and that guarantee can be given industry only if the government intend to adopt a sane financial policy that will maintain in Canada at all times an effective demand against our production. Is the government prepared to give industry the assurance that it will underwrite an effective demand in this country, so that there will be in Canada a ready market for our total production or the production of other nations for which our own production can be exchanged? If this is not done, then it will retard our production and considerably delay the time when these controls can be lifted, because no industry can continue to expand production unless it has at the same time an expanding market.
The next important point is this: What effect is the government's taxation policy having upon production in this country, upon the secondary industries, upon primary industry and upon labour? I think the answer in every case must be that their taxation policy has retarded production. I know that is certainly true so far as agriculture is concerned. It is true in regard to mixed farming, grain farming, and the production of live stock. Again, as the production of this country expands, is the government prepared to reduce drastically the taxation on the people in the lower income brackets so as to help to maintain an effective demand?
I would say that unless this government intends to deal very rapidly with the points I have raised it is also bound to delay the day on which these controls can be removed. Yet, on the other hand, I would ask this question: How can the government hope to underwrite the full development of the resources of the country and at the same time reduce taxation without plunging us still further into the morass of debt? Unless of course they intend to adopt a sane financial policy such as that outlined by the Prime Minister in 1935, when he said that currency and credit would be made available in terms of public need to meet the domestic and social requirements of the Canadian people, it cannot be done.
It may be said that the government have done that in the war. To a certain extent that is true, but you must remember that it was done by expanding the national debt by over ten billions, and no one would suggest that this can be considered a sane policy for peace time. While therefore we want a policy that will make sufficient money available to maintain effective demand against the production of our country, we want it done on a 47696-187
basis that will not at the same time expand our debt. Notwithstanding anything I have sa_'d, I am not suggesting for one minute the elimination of all controls. Some controls should be considered a permanent part of government policy for all time; for example, the control of foreign exchange in order to prevent gambling in foreign exchange, in order to prevent large-scale foreign investment abroad, which can only result in one of two things: either an unbalanced trade or a lower standard of living for the Canadian people.
We definitely favour a degree of price control in primary products in order to guarantee the farmer a fair share of the national income, so that the farmer's income may bear the same relationship to the national income as the farm population does the national population. Therefore we favour at all times a floor under primary products, and it should be based on parity prices, thereby helping to bring about a fairer distribution of income as between the primary and secondary industries.
I would emphasize this. Because ever since 1935 we in this group have consistently, year in and year out, advocated a degree of price control, and that was one of the main planks of the platform of the Social Credit party in Alberta in that year. We hear a lot of talk about free enterprise and free markets. I would point out that this condition has not existed in this country for as long as I can remember. It ended with the coming into being of combines, trusts, cartels, trade unions -and I am not attacking trade unions-and fixed overhead debt charges. Every one of these resisted the operation of free enterprise, therefore we need controls to prevent its abuse. The idea of free enterprise and markets was based on the understanding mat there should be no government interference in prices; that prices were governed by the laws of supply and demand; that when supply, exceeded demand prices would fall until the balance was restored and vice versa; that when demand exceeded supply, prices would rise and absorb the difference. AVhat has happened? Does anybody suggest for one minute that that is what has happened in the past? When supply exceeded effective demand, whilst the prices of primary products fell, the prices of the secondary goods, although registering a slight fall, were quickly stabilized by the secondary industries reducing production in order to meet the reduced buying power. That was done instead of reducing prices. Therefore it is nonsense to suggest that we have had free enterprise in operation in this country. Had the purchasing power of the people been maintained so that there

National Emergency

should be an effective demand against production, prices need not have fallen and production need not have been reduced. Therefore, so long as the government maintains the present system price, controls will be essential in order to assure a parity living cost between the primary and secondary industries of this country, and, consequently, labour.
Generally speaking I believe the government have made a good job of maintaining controls during the war. I want to be fair in making that statement. Of course we all know that mistakes have been made, but considering the circumstances they might very easily have been far greater. I find that the main demand for the removal of all controls does not come from the great mass of the people but from the heads of certain corporations who want freedom to exploit the people. The people of this country endured the inconvenience of those controls during the war because they recognized they were essential. Surely it would be better to put up with them for a few more months than prematurely to lift them and cause a chaotic state of affairs in the country. Again I want to emphasize the fact that if that happens it will not be the wealthy people who will suffer, but mainly the veterans and their dependents and the people in the lower income brackets. Nevertheless I say that it is important for the government to realize that the people will not tolerate the extension of those controls for one day longer than is necessary.	.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, parliament is now being asked to give through or by legal status almost what amounts to blanket powers of control over what in the end will mean the lives and destiny of the Canadian people. I have listened with considerable interest to the observations that have so far been made in this present debate, and many valuable points have been brought out both in favour of and against the measure. I find that those who seem to be in favour of the measure base much of their argument on the fact that because of certain present circumstances for which we cannot be responsible, it is advisable to grant the government an extension of time in matters of control. On the other hand I think I can say that those who desire to argue against the bill argue on the basis of the principle which is involved, and it is upon that basis that I should like to argue to-day.
It is all very well for those of us of the opposition to be asked: "What would you do if you were in power?" Perhaps that is a reasonable question, but the fact remains that we are not in power. The fact remains that

under our parliamentary system we are not members of the government, but members of His Majesty's most loyal opposition. As members of that opposition it is not our duty to say what we would do if we were in power. It is our duty to bring out the weaknesses of His Majesty's loyal government and to seek to peruse and investigate every detail of legislation which His Majesty's government proposes, bring out its weak spots and warning the government and the people of Canada of the dangers we see in it. I believe that is what we are here for. The argument, what did you do under certain circumstances, was made last night. The Conservative party were referred to, and certain legislation which they passed when they were in power was quoted. I am certain that we could refer to the (Speeches which were made at that time by the present Prime Minister, who was then leader of His Majesty's most loyal opposition. I wonder what he would have said at that time about such legislation as this. Overnight I have not been able to make an analysis of all those speeches; I have not even looked at the index of Hansard to find out where they appear, but I am certain that the present Prime Minister did not attack it as he would if he had been in power. If he opposed the bill he opposed it because he had a duty to perform as leader of His Majesty's opposition.
I shpuld like to discuss the measure on the basis of what I believe to be the principle involved. In the first place I suggest that the government is asking for almost omnipotent power. It is Canada's responsible government which is asking for this power, and I feel impelled to ask, to whom is the government responsible? Is it responsible to big business? Is it responsible to some unseen backstage powers, or is it responsible to the people of Canada? Technically, of course, the answer is that; it is responsible to the people of Canada, but in practice it seems to me that it assumes it is responsible to a government which is more responsible than it is, namely, a government of a mighty financial tyranny.
I am going to refer to something that was said the other day. I cannot quote from Hansard because it was during another debate, but I recall that at the time a little argument was going on between someone on this side of the house, the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). They were talking about coal, and the Minister of Labour described the economic cost factors involved in the mining of coal in Canada as compared to the mining of coal in the United States. Then he went on to say that when conditions eventually reached a normal state the price of coal-and I want

National Emergency
hon. members to get this-then would be the determining factor, that it would not matter very much where it came from. To him the question was very complex, and it seemed that he was alarmed because at the very moment he was speaking we could buy coal from West Virginia for much less than we could buy coal from Nova Scotia. Then I recall he made this remark, because I made a little note of it; he said, "That is an alarming situation, and you cannot wish yourself out of a jam like that." He hoped the coal commission would have an answer.
What was the principle involved in that? The principle was that the money system, with its complex construction of cost factors, trade and so forth, was his master; that there was an unseen government inherent in the present financial system which did not leave this government free to do what it wanted to do; that the present monetary system controlled the policy of the government. Now, what am I getting at? I am simply saying that a government which is already controlled now is asking parliament to give it power to operate under a system which is more powerful than it is. As members of the opposition we can take to task a government which has not received power from us; but when we give it the power and it in turn becomes subject to a higher power, where does it leave parliament? To my mind that is the principle involved. There is an unseen power of financial circumstance, and in the past the government have refused to face the physical facts squarely and then apply the remedy. Rather they have listened to the voices of proteges of the big bosses of finance; and because they have listened to those voices they have become grooved, rutted, bogged in the mire of financial circumstances inherent in the imminent breakdown of a faulty financial system.
The principle involved is this: that to make the system #ork they must have power to apply some force; and under the terminology of controls, shall I say, they are seeking power. Let us not fool ourselves on this. They do not say they want controls; they want power. They want parliament, the representatives of the people, to delegate power to them. The whole scheme abroad, not only here in Canada but throughout the world to-day, is a scheme to force the present financial tyranny to work. Therefore governments need power. What do they want power for? Do they want power to change the present system? I doubt that very much. They want power to fall in line, to keep in step with all other governments under the same financial tyranny; power to make it work, instead of power to change 47696-187J
the system. Last evening the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was talking about nerve. Well, it does not require very much nerve for a clerk in a store to tell his understudies what to do.- It does take nerve for that same clerk to say to his boss, "You are wrong; you are stupid; you are a crook, and I am not going to do the thing you want me to do because there is a principle involved." That is the kind of nerve the government should have.
The minister said quite a lot about nerve. Well, during the war I think the government did have some nerve, but it was of a different kind. They had nerve when they put over a plebiscite on this country and then did not put into operation what the country told them to put into operation. That was pretty nervy. It went beyond nerve; it was cheek. They certainly had nerve to fire their minister of national defence and then the next day turn around and do what he had told them to do. That was nervy; it was cheek. I will tell you what the government can do if they want to show their nerve. They can tell their financial advisers, whom I sometimes call intellectual dry-rots, that for once in their terms of office they are going to face the physical facts and change the present system to fit those facts. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that in connection with legislation already passed by parliament and legislation still on the order paper, if we could only take a little peek behind the scenes we would discover that much of it is being passed at the circumstantial dictates of a power much greater than the government who now sit in office.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words to justify my attitude in regard to bill No. 15. Having received letters from many people in my constituency who do not approve this bill, I should like to point out publicly the reasons why I am in favour of it.
Before going any further I admit that I do not like any more than anybody else these orders in council which give or delegate powers to a bureaucracy who are not in any way responsible to the people. On the other hand, everybody will admit that we are facing a situation which has practically no precedent. The present session is getting near its end. We cannot expect the members to stay in continuous session to take care of any emergency which may arise from time to time. So

National Emergency
authority of some kind must be delegated to some body to deal with the matter in the absence of the members.
I shall confine my remarks on the bill to its essence or spirit, without going into the details of the sections. At present, as everybody knows, there is such an acute shortage of goods not only in this country but all over the world that if there were no controls at all, prices would reach a ceiling never thought of. What would happen then? The poor people would be deprived of the necessities of life. What I have said regarding prices of goods applies as well to wages.
It has been said in this house that this bill No. 15 jeopardizes the rights of the provinces. But if we had to wait for the provinces to take action in the matter and control the situation it wrould certainly take a long time, during which the people of this country would suffer.
I will admit that drastic legislation such as that outlined in this bill is not agreeable to the people of this country, but action must be taken to protect the people, even if they do not like to be protected. It is the duty of the authorities to do it. When a person has to undergo a surgical operation he does not stop to think whether he likes it or not; it simply has to be done. I consider that the government has to perform a surgical operation presently for the benefit of the people of Canada, and if the government did not take the proper means to do it, it would not be justifying the confidence which the people have put in their representatives.
I would respectfully draw the attention of hon. members of this house to the fact that these remarks of mine are against my own interest. If I had my personal interest in mind I should vote against the bill, because the foreign markets are interested in buying certain goods that are made in Canada, and I could dispose at a premium of the goods which are produced in factories in which I am interested. As a matter of fact I could sell in the United States and South American countries many times the quantity of goods which I manufacture and of which the export is now prohibited. This goes to prove that it is against my own interest to favour legislation such as is outlined in bill No. 15. But I understand that as a member of parliament I must forget my own interest for the benefit of the public at large. That is the reason why I shall vote in favour of bill No. 15.
Before taking my seat I am proud to pay a tribute of admiration to the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) for acting in such a virile manner in presenting this bill under such adverse circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly unfortunate that the government should have waited until the last days of the session to introduce this most important bill, the passing of which may entail very grave consequences from a constitutional standpoint. Now that we have to sit from eleven o'clock in the morning to eleven in the evening, besides having to attend committee sittings, it is obvious that we cannot devote to the study of this measure all the attention which its importance demands. It will perhaps be said that the bill has been on the order paper for a long time, but everyone knows what that means, since it has been decided that consideration of some measures which had been put on the order paper would be left until other sessions. A bill can only be discussed when it has been introduced in the house.
At all events, I do not intend to prolong this debate too much and I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible in the few remarks I have to make. Besides, I believe that the speeches delivered by the hon. members for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), for Beauhamois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) and for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) have covered the various aspects of the problem we have to solve.
I have also listened with deep interest to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage). Of course, I cannot agree with most of what he said, but he has also made a particular remark which has my entire support, and I think it is proper that I should quote it. The hon. member for Montmagny-LTslet said, as reported on page 2919 of Hansard.
I do not feel that the people of my constituency gave me a mandate merely to pass that mandate over to the government.
I am in perfect agreement with the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet on that point. When I had the honour of being elected to represent the electors of Charlevoix-Saguenay, it was certainly not for the purpose of handing over to the governor in council all the powers devolved on the government of this country.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the matter which is now before us is most important. It is important because it affects the very basis of the confederation pact. Indeed, I think I am justified in adding that in the past, when differences arose between the provincial authorities and the dominion government, it was almost in every instance upon the interpretation of sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. Now, this bill involves those two sections; in other words, it is intended to transfer within the powers of the
National Emergency

dominion parliament certain provincial rights and powers defined in section 92 of the B.N.A. Act. Hence, I contend that the matter is very important, I repeat, it may have far-reaching and altogether disastrous consequences. Instead of bombastic speeches of the type made last night by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I should have preferred sounder and more weighty arguments in support of the government's point of view. Among the few principles set forth by the Minister of Agriculture, one of them stood out more prominently than the others; I refer to his quotation of a business man's opinion on the matter. At this point, Mr. Speaker, let me state the viewpoint of Mr. Burton, President of the Robert Simpson Company of Toronto, another business man well known all over the country. According to Le Devoir of October 12, 1945, Mr. Burton said, in relation to bill No. 15:
At present, Ottawa is devising the collapse of reconversion, and Canada's future is at stake. Bill 15 sets forth emergency powers more extensive than those vested in cabinet during the war.	'
Controls, instead of being curtailed, are extended to new fields. Now that hostilities are over, the privileges sought in the bill are no longer necessary; in fact, they would entail a severe menace. The act is to continue in force for a period of twelve months, but this type of legislation is usually renewed from year to year.
Civil liberties and property rights are imperli-led, and if bill 15 is passed, the provinces will be stripped of their constitutional prerogatives. The freedom of every Canadian citizen is thus affected.
I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that if the matter discussed in the house for the past couple of days had been thrashed out before a fair-minded court, the arguments submitted by the hon. members for Stanstead and Beauhamois-Laprairie would have won hands down over those set forth by the hon. members sitting on the right.
Personally, I wish to point out only a few specific features of the bill now before us. Incidentally, if in so doing I have the good fortune to reflect the opinion of the electorate in the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay, well and good; some people may claim that I am making an election speech, but that is irrelevant, for I shall have the satisfaction of knowing that I have done my duty. Therefore, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that national unity is endangered by this bill.

entity of this country when they are usurped by the other entity. I say that such is not the menace with which we are threatened at present, but the present menace may be more dangerous because it attacks the Canadian confederation in its very foundation. We are threatened with a conflict between provincial autonomy and the federal government. In order to mitigate the consequences of the bill, it is often said and contended that it is but a transitional measure which would grant powers to the governor in council for a period of one year only. This is not accurate. If one examines section 6 of the new bill he finds that the powers granted to the governor in council will extend until next session; it is therefore evident, from the text of the bill itself, that the said powers are given to the governor in council for more than a year, at least for one year and three or four months. But how long the bill remains in effect is not important. The situation would still be the same were the powers granted to the governor in council for a few months only. A principle is involved and not a question of time. I submit that it is exclusively a matter of principle and it is in that light that we should look at the bill which is now before us. On the other hand, the principle, the basis of that bill has been the subject of earlier discussions in the house. For instance, this happened during a debate when, during * the second special session of 1930, the Bennett government having just attained power, a session was called in order to authorize the governor in council to spend $20,000,000 to ward off the disastrous results of unemployment which prevailed at that time. If I refer to the House of Commons Debates for the special session of 1930, I find certain statements which I believe should be remembered diming the present debate. For instance, on page 178 I note the following statement:
Last night in speaking to the resolution on which this bill is based he said that we had no right to ignore the needs of suffering humanity. May I tell him in a spirit of absolute sincerity and humility that there are many of us on this side of the house who through birth and struggle have probably a better appreciation of the struggles of the labouring people of Canada. Let me tell him that he has no right to assume that because we are here protecting the fundamental rights and privileges of parliament he has any monopoly of sympathy with the sufferings of humanity.
Those words were uttered 'by the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) during the special session of 1930.
Further on, the hon. minister stated:
The leader of the government knows as well as anyone in this house that the struggle for responsible government in England since the
i

National Emergency
days of Edward I has been the struggle on the part of the people's representatives to secure full and final -control over every cent of money expended. Further, the hon. gentleman knows quite well that as a result of the constitutional struggle of 1910 in the old land the final financial control of the House of Commons was completely established. The same principle holds in Canada.
As reported on page 258 of Hansard of that same 1930 session, he went on:
My plea to the -house is this:	Leave the
authority to parliament. Having been sent here by the Canadian people, we have obligations and responsibilities to them. It does not matter much which party claims our allegiance; the people who sent us here have placed certain obligations upon our shoulders. iSo far -as I am concerned, therefore, not even to protect any industry in the country, not even the fruit industry of British Columbia, shall I stand for the infringement of the -rights of parliament and for.delegating to any cabinet, even the almighty, all-powerful Conservative government, the power which belongs to parliament.

To me this is not so much Tory legislation as it is Soviet control in the Dominion of -Canada.
I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will not add to the poverty of their argument the intolerance of interruption. You will be asked to approve a measure to extend certain specified emergency powers to meet emergency conditions in the period of -reconstruction.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what happened since the day on which the speech from the throne
was read by the governor general, a speech in which the -bill now before the house for granting the government certain powers was announced? What could have happened between this day and the 23rd of November when bill No. 15 was introduced in the House of Commons?

Indeed if the government had introduced a bill as was forecast in the speech from the throne it would have meant that these gentlemen would have been deprived of the dictatorial powers they have enjoyed for too long. That has been done, -and important

'amendments have been drafted which we believe and expect will help to meet the objections that have been raised, and incidentally help to meet objections that otherwise might have been raised by hon. gentlemen opposite.
By way of digression, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that in his statement the right honourable the prime minister perhaps said too much, but certainly did not say enough. He mentioned the objection raised by a few prime ministers. Now, inasmuch as the matter has been referred to the prime ministers of the nine provinces of the dominion and since it was the right honourable the prime minister himself who gave that information to the house of commons, we should, I think, havre a right to know who are the prime ministers who raised objections and who are those, if any, who agreed to bill No. 15 in its original form.
