Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to comply with your wishes. I will confine myself to the Prime Minister's statement which I quoted a short while ago. I should like to say that the bill as amended, which was submitted to the house afer the Prime Minister said that he had agreed to incorporate certain changes at the request of the provincial premiers, is, in some of its features, even worse than the first draft.
In fact, if we examine bill 15, I think I am justified in saying that it has a dual purpose. The first seeks to grant the governor in council, through parliament, powers which, under section 92 of the British North America Act, belong by right to the provincial legislatures. The second asks parliament to abdicate all control it may be entitled to exercise over the affairs of the country and to vest these rights in the governor in council.
The powers of the first category were clearly set forth recently by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) when he introduced the bill to the house. The following excerpt is quoted from page 2452 of Hansard:
One of the important questions for the consideration of the house is this question of fact: Is it or is it not true that some matters normally of provincial jurisdiction have 'aspects at this time which are other than their normal aspects as dealt with in the subsections of section 92 of the British North America Act?
And a bit further on:
Are we still in a condition of national emergency such as to affect the distribution of legislative powers between the dominion and the

National Emergency
provinces, and, as a practical proposition, such as to affect what should he the distribution of legislative functions as between parliament and the governor in council?
Well, these are the very questions to which the members of the government have not replied satisfactorily. In fact, the Minister of Justice quoted in support of his argument a ruling made by the Privy Council when the case of The Manitoba Free Press Company was referred to it; this ruling, as reported in a speech by the Minister of Justice, appearing in Hansard of November 23, states the following:
Where an exact line of demarcation will lie in such cases'it may not be easy to lay down a priori, nor is it necessary. For in the solution of the problem regard must be had to the broadened field covered, in case of exceptional necessity, by the language of section 91, in which the interests of the dominion generally are protected.
Therefore, it is apparent in the ruling quoted by the Minister of Justice that only in case of exceptional necessity, may we strip the provinces of the rights conferred upon them under section 92 of the B.N.A. Act.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no weighty arguments and no sound proofs have been given in support of the contention that these really exceptional needs do exist. The bill in its present form, as introduced in the house, should have been first submitted to the provincial governments, for, at a time when the federal authorities are seeking the cooperation of all provincial legislatures in its attempt to reorganize our economic system, if parliament passes legislations on matters of such vital interest to the provinces as those contemplated in the present bill, the procedure adopted in this instance is a lack of confidence and, I might say, an insult to them, and this is not the proper way to promote cooperation on the part of the provincial bodies. Therefore, as a matter of justice, and in the interest of negotiations which are to be pursued between the federal and provincial governments, I claim that, as the federal authorities wish to be successful in implementing the policy they have expounded, it is necessary and appropriate for them to submit such projected measures to the provincial governments.
As to the assignment of powers we are requested to approve, it is purely a surrender of our control over certain matters into the hands of the governor in council.
I say that in the present circumstances we have no right to do so. I contend that it has not been satisfactorily proven to us that we have the right to grant to the governor in council the powers requested by bill No. 15. And, as a consequence of this claim, I say 47696-188
that if this bill is passed by Parliament, the law will be ultra vires and may be annulled at any time by courts of justice. Should a dispute arise as a result of this measure, I say that we may well see a repetition of what happened in 1935 and 1936 when several laws enacted by the Bennett government in 1934 and 1935 were set aside by the Privy Council.
It has been repeated time and again during the present debate, that we must admit in spite of all that there is a great necessity of maintaining certain controls and certain regulations passed under the War Measures Act.
I do not say, Mr. Speaker, that the whole structure set up in the past few years through orders in council and measures of all kinds should be demolished at a single blow, but I say that there are constitutional means of remedying this situation. If we had asked the provincial premiers last week to legislate on matters within their jurisdiction in order to maintain certain controls, I believe, if I judge from the atmosphere which prevailed at that conference, that we would have been supported by all the provincial premiers who would have agreed to legislate in the special cases within their own jurisdiction.
As for the second category of powers which I mentioned a while ago, if we had been called upon during the present session to approve definite and specific legislation dealing with the continuation of certain controls and regulations during the reconversion period, I am almost sure that no objections would have been raised in the house, because nearly everyone recognizes that some of the present controls should be maintained.
(Text).
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to sum up my remarks as follows: My contention is that the bearing of this bill is twofold, or should I say that there are two categories of powers provided in this bill. First, the government is asking for authority to deal with matters pertaining to provincial powers. Second, the government is asking parliament to authorize it to make legislation by orders in council.
As regards the first category, now that we know the government has thought fit to submit to the provincial premiers the project of this bill, we ought.to know if this new bill No. 15, as reprinted, meets with the approval of the premiers. The government should give us the evidence that the premiers of the provinces have agreed to this new bill; otherwise. in all fairness and equity, and I may say, in all decency, the proposed amendments should not be presented.

National Emergency

As regards the second category of powers, my contention is that this parliament does not possess the right to authorize the government to govern this country by orders in council. I believe this bill, should it become law, would be ultra vires of the powers of this parliament, and I do not hesitate to state that in a judicial case emanating from this law, our courts would come to the conclusion that it is ultra vires and illegal. One may reply that, even if we admit this point of view, we must also be aware of the fact that some of the measures adopted under the War Measures Act cannot easily be rescinded immediately I am ready to agree to that, but I suggest that this bill is not at all a proper remedy for this situation. What the government should do would be to ask the provincial governments to pass the necessary legislation dealing with the problems pertaining to their constitutional authority; and from what we were told about the interprovincial conference I believe the premiers would be willing to accept this suggestion.
As regards the first category of powers already mentioned, I would suggest that the government submit to parliament special and precise legislation which would cover the needs of the present period, but nothing else. Therefor, my contention is not only that this bill is ultra vires, but that we do not need it; and there is only one way out, which is by way of the following amendment. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi:
That in the motion now before the house the word "now" be left out and the words "this day six months" added at the end of the question.
Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil) (Translation)-: Mr. Speaker, as the majority of the hon. members do not speak French, I shall speak in English.
(Text).
Victory over the enemies of freedom having been won by our people, Mr. Speaker,, at an untold price in lives and sacrifices of all kinds, every Canadian worthy of the name has become tremendously interested in the preservation of his political liberties and the democratic processes of government which he has come to cherish so dearly. The average Canadian believes, rightly or wrongly, that the institutions he fought for and for which his sons died will cope with the problems arising out of this complete but costly victory; and he has faith in his elected representatives, feeling that the difficulties arising within the immediate post-war period will be settled to his satisfaction, according to his conception of responsible government. Even to superficial thinkers it must appear abundantly clear that this parliament is faced with vast and

complicated problems, weighty and huge, growing in immensity as new conditions arise. The bill before this house transcends party interests and immediate political advantage, and I for one would not care to consider this bill in the light of political colour. This bill, more than any other measure brought before this house during the present session, (including the flag question on which we could not even agree in principle) shows fully the varying trends of thought in this country, the difficulty of interpreting our constitution in time of war or economic stress, and how very finely balanced is our confederation. All of us here are sworn to serve the best interests of our country, and only those of bad faith would dare question the sincerity of their fellow members. We are all seeking to attain the same end, a united, prosperous, sovereign Canada; yet each of us may in all good faith differ from his fellow members as to the means of attaining that end.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not at all scandalized by the speeches which have been made on this bill, whether they came from my personal friend, the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon); whether they came from the batonnier general of the Quebec bar, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), with whose speech I entirely agree; whether they came from the hon. member for Beau-harnois (Mr. Raymond), who offered a very strong indictment against the bill; whether they came from the hon. member for Beauoe (Mr. Dionne), whom I had to persuade all morning to make his maiden speech in this house, or whether they came from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who, as "the old reliable", made a laudable effort to try and convince this house that this country has a good government. All these speeches show that we are breathing freedom, that we are living and working toward democracy. Ever since Lord Durham's report there has been a conflict of political thought in Canada; yet our country has prospered and developed almost progressively with this conflict of thought. Personally, and I say this with all due respect, I attach as much importance to the speeches and gestures made by Papineau and the grandfather of the present Prime Minister as I would attach to those of Sir John Colborne and his lieutenants. Their actions might have been diametrically opposed, yet they were directed toward the same end; and to those factions we owe the responsible government we are enjoying to-day.
Our struggle for responsible government has been long, arduous and costly. This bill is just another measure which literally throws back into the laps of legislators the responsi-, bility of maintaining responsible government.

National Emergency
Shall we have economic control or shall we have economic freedom? That is the question. To all true lovers of liberty, urgent as this bill might appear to be, the underlying principle is repugnant, if I may use that word. Those who have sacrificed loved ones on the altar of liberty in the hope that the price paid would not be too high, attach great importance to that one attribute which establishes the difference between democracy and dictatorship, between free men and chained men. To those of us who worship at freedom's altar this bill is a dark and overwhelming question mark. Yet we must face hard facts, Mr. Speaker. Our economy is dangerously unbalanced. We have switched from agriculture to industry as a major occupation, and all our old theories as to supply and demand, freedom of enterprise and endeavour, have gone by the board. Let us admit it. Our participation in this war has given our economic skeleton, if I may use that expression, a terrific shock from which we may not soon recover. This house now is being asked to sanction a measure conferring upon the governor-in-couneil transitional powers during the national emergency arising out of the war. We are not told by what yardstick Jhe transition will be measured, nor are we informed of the scope and extent of the emergency. If we were asked to sanction specific controls, fully described and demonstrated, I think it would be easier for all of us to accept the measure.
Unfortunately this bill is uncertain in its portent, like many other bills which have been presented during the present session. No one in his senses will deny the necessity of certain controls, but every disciple of freedom will challenge an unlimited mandate to the governor-in-council to legislate without consulting in advance the elected representatives of the people. If we are, and we are, a government of the people for the people, we cannot for any reason, however weighty it may appear, surrender our vested powers to any other authority, however respected it may be. This is a time as never before to reestablish the supremacy of parliament over an irresponsible bureaucracy which this war inevitably created and which the might of our war effort may have justified. I want to be fair about that. The more this parliament surrenders its powers to a bureaucracy which is not responsible to the people, the more this parliament will lose the respect of those same people. After all, it was not the bureaucracy which stood the last general election ; it was all of us here. The old civil service did more than its share during the war, without any addi-47690-1884
tional wages. It is that new bureaucracy which came in to win the war at any price that we should guard against.
Edmund Burke, that great English parliamentarian, speaking on conciliation with America, made this statement which I would ask h'on. members to bear in mind:
As long as you have the wisdom to keep sovereign authority of this country as the sanctuary of liberty, the sacred temple consecrated to our common faith, wherever our chosen race and sons of our country worship freedom, they will turn their faces toward you . . . Deny them this participation of freedom and you break that sole bond which originally made and must still preserve the unity of our empire. It is the spirit of the English constitution which, infused through the mighty mass, feeds, unites, invigorates, vivifies eyery part of the empire, even down to the minutest member.
Another delicate question, Mr. Speaker, is involved in this bill, namely the conflict of federal and provincial powers. I know of no province more willing than my own to cooperate with the federal authorities. Yet, because of its racial, linguistic, economic, geographic, social and even sentimental peculiarities, the province of Quebec is justifiably jealous of its autonomy and justifiably worried as "to the loss of its essential powers. On this subject I want to state further that the influential and much respected English-speaking minority in my province has expressed itself as sharing the1 same views, since it feels that well enough should be left alone.
May I give a word of warning, to the house? Broken friendships, must not lie ahead if we are to become more united; and no province or group must look hopelessly to the future feeling that it has been betrayed. Controls have weighed very heavily upon our people, and I want to accentuate that there is a general desire that these controls should disappear, unless urgency demands that they be maintained. On the principle that the preamble to this bill, instead of extending the freedom which has been promised ever since war was declared, further strangulates that same freedom, I cannot accept it. But I wish to make this reservation:	I shall gladly, however,
vote for any specific measure of control, if its necessity is demonstrated.
These are my last words: Canadians were not born to be controlled. Our forefathers came to this country because they were searching for freedom. Our fathers fought to maintain freedom, and our own kith and kin fought in this war to save it. I am prepared to go on record as stating that I still prefer to rely upon the qualities of recovery inherent in all true Canadians rather than upon a state-controlled economy conceived and directed
National Emergency

by irresponsible bureaucrats. And, Mr. Speaker, I would be prepared to go to the polls tomorrow on that sole issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I- believe this debate could have been shorter. Basically there is very little in the bill to which objection could be taken.
One has to have a thick skin to listen to all of the pleas for democracy and all the condemnations against dictatorships coming from people who, when war came along, opposed any idea of control of profits, while calling for all sorts of control of labour and wages. These same people, when it comes to the problem of tariffs and protection, are willing to have all sorts of government interference so that they may have sufficient profits. However in a matter which affects all the people, all of a sudden they become great defenders of democracy, as they understand it.
At present we are in a state of emergency so far as the problems of peace are concerned. There are many difficult problems, and hon. members in all quarters of the house-I have heard it from the start to the finish in various speeches from hon. members-realize that there is a peace emergency, a problem of finding jobs for people, a problem of creating work, a problem of making sure that there will be houses for the people, a problem of controlling prices and of wages.
I am sure hon. members who are opposed to this measure would gladly have a control of wages, but they would not like the control of prices-that is, they would agree to some controls, but not to others. I hold in my hand a letter which seems best to express the reason why there is so much opposition to this measure. This letter was received this morning from La Ligue des Proprietaires de Montreal -the league of proprietors of Montreal-and is as follows:
Bill 15, as amended, is now before the house. We earnestly beg that a clause be inserted in the bill providing that property owners be restored the rights to which they are entitled and which were suspended during the war, in order that their property may afford them more profitable earnings.
In a few words this letter tells us that we must see to it that the bill contains a section guaranteeing proprietors greater income. That is, it must do away with rental control and the freezing of leases, so that they may throw people out when they want to. All this despite the fact that there is *a shortage of houses in Montreal. But this is what they want to have done so they may raise rents a little higher. And let me assure hon. members that, despite rental controls, rents are high in Montreal.
[Mr. Heon.l
Someone told me recently that as much as S60 for a furnished room has been asked in that city. Without controls they would ask a rental of $100 or $150. They are very much interested in freedom, as they understand it- a freedom to fleece people, and take their last penny away from them.
I realize there have been abuses, and many of them. Small business men have come to me and told me that they could not get cloth, when the big business outfits had cloth. Used car dealers have told me that they were told they would have to close their yards in which they were selling second-hand cars, because they did not have shops to carry out repairs. Substandard wages have been frozen. No doubt there have been many other abuses. But basically we must agree that some measures are necessary at the present time.
Let no one dare to raise the constitutional problem. That problem has been raised again and again against the interests of the Canadian people. Some say, "Oh, you must not overstep the provincial rights of the provinces." What do they mean? They mean jvtst this: "Leave us alone and we will handle problems in the interests of a few wealthy people." Every time the federal government wishes to do something, those people in the provinces take this stand: "We will soon block them by the holler of provincial rights and constitutional rights." We hear lots of that in Quebec. I know that the premier of our province is one of the loudest in those statements. He has also told the proprietors at their conferences that he is opposed to all controls, and 'believes they should be able to charge all sorts of rates. That is what they have in mind. It is property rights in which they are interested-not the rights of the people. When they raise the cry of constitutional rights it is because they are thinking of the few, not of the people. In that spirit, Mr. Speaker, I support the bill and urge other members to support it.

Mr. Speaker, it is a little unexpected that I should be taking part in this debate on bill No. 15 because I saw by this morning's paper that bill No. 15 is virtually dead, but as the house is still debating it I shall join in the post mortem.
Bill No. 15 has been discussed by a great many members, especially members of the legal profession. One hon. member said yesterday that this bill controlled everything except going to church. He missed one thing. It does not take over control of the law business in Canada. It may be because the bill was drafted by a lawyer; I do not know.

National Emergency
But I think that those of us who are laymen, not legally-minded, should examine the bill from a layman's standpoint, because as you know, Mr. Speaker, the legal profession probably has the lowest batting average of any profession, for half of its members lose their cases.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: But this half is absolutely right.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
This bill is to endorse and continue the wartime controls and government by order in council. To that we take strong exception. We admit that controller-ships were necessary during the war, but undoubtedly they provoked a lot of animosity, and they will provoke more if continued in peace time. I have been thinking about a controllership right in this house. I moved down to this seat from the back row because there were three shadows on my desk and I could hardly see a thing. I saw the whip, the controller of lighting, and the Sergeant at Arms. I think we need a "shadow"' controller to fix it .up. However, with all the discomforts of my seat it is not nearly as uncomfortable as the seats of hon. members will be who vote in favour of this bill.
The house has discussed controllerships at length, and I shall not take up much time on that. We have discussed housing, which is run by boards and bureaucrats. Somebody had the idea that the veterans should be put on an acre of land instead of becoming city citizens and being assimilated in the general citizenship of Canada, and so they bought a lot of farms and established soldier settlements. That all comes from having too many controllers, each one trying to run his own department.
I do not necessarily represent any party in speaking about controllers. The people I am thinking of are the people of Canada, the business men, the farmers, the labouring men. There is no use telling the Canadian working man that he is better off than the Russian or Australian or British worker, because the Canadian working man wants to be better off than the Canadian working man. More power to him! He wants his own lot to be better. It cannot be better under a bill of this kind, because on whatever other subject you may legislate you cannot legislate human nature, and this bill diametrically opposes human nature because it kills incentive and initiative. "Controllers" remind me of the lighthouse-keeper on the coast who had been keeping the light for thirty years, with the fog horn sounding every two minutes. He woke up in the middle of the night when the fog horn had suddenly stopped sounding, and
said, "What was that?" Some of these controllers do not know that the guns have stopped firing; they do not know that the war is over; they do not know that these temporary buildings are not permanent buildings.
My objection to a bill of this kind is that it lends itself to creating more bureaucrats, more boards and more controls. Not long ago the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) said, at page 913 of Hansard:
As I have said, I have always felt that we have too many boards.
He went on to say:
I hope they go forward with the legislation that is on the statute hooks and not appoint a lot of boards.
But on that occasion he was talking against somebody else's resolution. Under bill No. 15 we are bound to have more boards and more controllers.
It is an old story that governments make their worst mistakes when they assume infallibility on their own part, or assume a lack of interest or ability on the part of the public, and endeavour to reduce parliament to impot-ency. Nothing is more important than to recognize our form of government and that the representatives of the people shall understand that a responsibility rests upon them to protect not only the rights and liberties of the people, but the institutions of sound representative government that have been slowly and painfully worked out over the years.
Another thing that this bill does through establishing bureaux and controllers and boards is to absorb too large a share of manpower working for the government. That takes more taxes from the people to keep this thing going, and the people could spend that money themselves much more wisely than in paying taxes for boards and controllers. Of course, I know that these orders in council lend themselves to schemes that appeal to certain groups, which if submitted to the people themselves would be quickly turned down.
We have discussed in this house collective bargaining and union security when speaking of the rights of labour. That is all right. But how about collective bargaining with the provinces? The provinces met with the dominion government last week, and the provinces have certain rights which they quite properly feel should be respected. This bill I understand has been amended because of representations that were. made by the provinces, but still the bill now 'before us seems to contain nearly everything objectionable ,that was in the original bill. The hon. member for Kindersl'ey (Mr. Jaenicke) said that he was going to support the principle of the

National Emergency
bill but would offer some amendments later. If you were going to build a house you would not build the house and then decide that you wanted the kitchen on the other end. You would make your changes in the blueprint. This bill is in the blueprint stageThen why not amend it and bring it in right? Why bring it before the committee of the whole to have the amendments made there? There are a lot of people in the government service who could draft a simple 'bill to cover what is required.
You have to use your imagination as a layman. I have no personal hates. If you spend ten hours of your life on personal hates you would be much better off dying ten hours sooner. I used my imagination on this bill when it was introduced last week. I can visualize things just by thinking a little, and it seemed to me that the minister came in carrying a bouncing baby. He mentioned bread and milk and butter. In other words the baby needed bread, milk and butter. And to get bread, milk and butter for the baby we are to have all these boards and controls continued. That was carrying the baby on a political platform and asking the people to vote for it.
The Social Credit party have spoken on this bill and stated that the government was asking parliament to set aside the constitution and to continue controllers and boards. Everybody took the same attitude on the original bill," so naturally when I came back from Montreal yesterday I expected to find a short one-page bill before the house. However, I did not find it. I agree also with the thought expressed not very long ago by the minister who introduced this bill. He is a gentleman whom we all like and for whose ideas we have a good deal of respect. He wap talking about another resolution, and he said something to this effect: To pass this resolution in the terms in which it is drawn would be an abdication of the rights and privileges of this house. He was-speaking of some other measure, but I agree with what he said, because we should preserve the rights of this house, and this bill No. 15' is a complete abdication of those rights. To me it looks as though you are just selling out our freedom, and I agree with what was said by an hon. member sitting to my left, that the principle of the thing was to give the government the power, and from then on we would not have any power ourselves. It is too much power to put in the hands of a few.
I have not the least idea, Mr. Speaker, that these ministers would exert all these powers, or take advantage of them; but why give the power to them?-because anything can happen

to people. These ministers might go out in a bus and fall in the river and get drowned. That is not wishful thinking. Anything can happen. Someone else might crawl in and get their power; someone else, regardless of what party he belonged to, might succeed to the throne or the power behind the throne and take advantage of this act. I do not think we should resign all our power, to be used, perhaps by undiscriminating people; and it must be remembered that politicians and governments are not permanent. I might drop over myself. Don't get optimistic; I feel fine. Surely, if this parliament is to have 245 members, that is not too many in whom to vest the power of parliament, because that conversely is equal representation of the people of Canada, and hon. members on our side and on the other side can judge as to what are necessary controls, and do so just as well as the government. We do not need to put all these controls in the hands of the cabinet.
This parliament represents the people. There are only 245 of us, of whom half are usually here, but that is none too many to have charge of these things. The faster we get rid of these controls, or determine that we shall get rid of these various boards and controls, the sooner we can proceed with reconversion. I do not agree with the government that reconversion cannot take place until 1948. I think we should resolve that we shall be reconverted next year. We might not make it, but let us try it. Not long ago a minister told us that the reason the 1948 figures were selected was that that was thought to be the first year in which we could safely estimate that there would be full conversion from war to peace. If you make the date 1948 you will probably reach your objective by 1950, because they cannot keep up to schedule. The war is over, and I think it is time to pass a little more authority and freedom back to the provinces, the municipalities, and the public.
We have been fighting a war many years. Nothing matters in war; human privileges are discarded in face of the enemy; you have to spearhead the attack by asking, by pleading, by forcing people to go one way, to do the job and carry on the fight. But now the enemy is beaten, and it behooves us to look at the people behind us. What do they expect? Why did they send us down here? What do they want? Do they want to be controlled continually as they were during the war? Do they want to be "run", to be told where to go, what to do, what they can have and what they cannot have; or do they want to return to some semblance of the democratic freedom they had before the war? To

National Emergency
get the answer to those questions one has only to turn to those who had boys overseas who fought and died, and to those who, having come back, expect to return to .a free Canada.
It seems to me that the government's function now is to unfetter the individual, to let him go to work and use his initiative, and he will do something.
I am not trying to condemn anybody particularly in connection with this bill, but I believe this is a time when all parties and all hon. members should be united for once. So far this session, it seems to me, the only thing on which we have been united is being disunited. That may be an Irishman's way of putting it. Here is something on which we all agree in our hearts; I am sure we do. What do our people want? They want to return to civil life and get on with their jobs. Well, jobs are not created by boards, except jobs for the controllers; they come from ideas. What is an idea? Well, I was concerned with one myself not so very long ago, when the electric refrigerator was a new idea. In 1920 I stood in the Toronto exhibition, and people looked at the exhibit and laughed at me and said, "It makes ice!" I was associated with the pioneers of the industry. They had to go to it and find money and help, build a factory and launch a business. It was a new idea, a new venture, but 860 of us had employment in that industry during the depression, when other fellows were out because they did not have ideas.
Now there are new industries coming along. I know of one United States corporation whose representatives came over to the London district about a month ago and looked over some property; they went to Ottawa, and examined the tax structure and the possibility of getting standard profits under the existing controls, and then gave up the idea of putting up a factory in Canada. I do not think this bill encourages industry, and I would say to my hon. friend to my left who took me to task one night that I do not mean the kind of industry which exploits labour.
An hon. C.C.F. MEMBER: There is no other.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The hon. member and
those who think as he does should let the workmen of Canada know that jobs cannot be created under a government-controlled plan, because government control kills all incentive and creative desires. We must get rid of war-time control and dictatorship, which I admit is necessary during war. The working men do not mind making more gadgets in eight hours than they ever made before if
they receive more for eight hours' work, because this enables them to get more out of life.
I do not say that we should take off every control to-morrow morning. 1 agree that we should continue a measure of price control, which means prices of services or goods, rationing of goods in short supply, and foreign exchange, but I do not think we should let it go beyond the point where it checks inflation and ensures a fair distribution of scarce goods. Parliament itself is just as well able to handle these controls as any board or cabinet. Incidentally the sooner we get back to sane thinking on these controls the better off we shall be.
I was inclined to be against this beautification scherpe for Ottawa when I heard about it, but if Doctor Greber will go ahead and take down these temporary buildings as the first part of his job, and so get rid of would-be permanent guests, I should be more in favour of the scheme. I was down in Washington on one occasion for three days with a gentleman who was connected with the Department of Munitions and Supply. The morning we got there a headline appeared in the paper, "President Roosevelt asks parasites to leave Washington." We did not know he saw us come in. I am not implying that these guests in the temporary buildings are parasites at all; they have worked hard, and done a grand job, but the longer you leave them there the less they will be needed, because their work is going to run out; so let us not encourage them to remain too long.
I am not necessarily speaking for my party, and I try to be non-political in my thinking. I have said that I have an imagination, and as I look down at my desk I seem to see my riding; I see London with its approximately
100,000	people. I do not represent the Progressive-Conservatives alone-at least I do not feel that I do. It is my job to come here as the representative of the constituency. I represent all parties, the voters and the non-voters, the women and the children. They want what they believe in and what they fought for-freedom to choose and freedom to live their lives, and I think we should make every effort-for all ridings are the same-to look after their interests and to do what they would like done.
Hon. members on the other side, if they vote against.this bill, are not going to defeat the government or cause a general election. On the other hand I would hesitate, regardless of what part of the house I sat in, before I would vote for this bill, because if I were on the government side, and not in the cabinet, it would seem to me to be a declaration to my
National Emergency

constituency that I was a weakling, not capable of handling the affairs of my,constituents or of taking their just part in government by a free parliament.
It seems to me that this is an opportunity for all hon. members to show their constituencies that they have their interests at heart, to assert that members have the stuff and stamina that they claim to have and that the people, when they sent them here, believed they had. and therefore voted for them. It would show their constituents that they are not frustrated, that they are 'not being run by the government, that they are not afraid to speak for the people, and that the will of Canadians will be done and a free parliament shall prevail. '
I do not believe that hon. members will desert the public opinion of their ridings. I am confident that if they realize {he principle involved, the principle of representative government and a free parliament, when the question is put there will be a thundering of "nays".

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I should like to associate myself with some of the remarks expressed this morning by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). One of his remarks was that members of the opposition, when we criticize and when we vote on any bill, we act more from the point of view of principle than from any technical viewpoint. I agree with that, and I am quite sure that is the way the people outside this house will interpret the vote of the opposition on this bill. Certainly previous speakers on this side of the house, opposition speakers, have made it clear that they at least are supporting or opposing the bill, one or the other, as a matter of principle, and I think I can say, in fact I know I can say, that this bill will have the support of all those who believe in state control and state planning. Well, I do not believe in either of those things, and neither do the people who sent me here, though I should say of course that I do not mean that everybody who votes for this bill necessarily believes in socialism. I am not saying that, but I do say that all those who believe in socialism will support this bill.
Some members have said that those who are opposed to the bill are taking orders from or studying the interests of those whom they call big shots. Let me say that I take my orders and my instructions only from those who honoured me with their confidence and their votes. I take orders from no one else. In that regard I have received several resolutions and a number of my constituents have instructed me to speak and oppose this bill to

the limits of my power. Nobody who wants me to support the bill has been good enough to tell me so, and therefore I will listen to those who have taken the trouble to write and tell me what they want. For these reasons I cannot support the bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had first of all a bill which we might call the original presented to parliament, and in connection with that bill the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke), speaking for our group, agreed with the principle that some powers which the government was seeking should be extended for a certain period of time and that we would vote for the measure on second reading and move certain definite amendments when the bill came into the committee stage. Subsequently the government undertook to amend its own bill and has presented us with a second bill which, as amended, is greatly improved over the original. Unfortunately the original bill is still before the house. It is a pity that the government did not withdraw that bill and present its amended bill as the measure to be discussed on second reading. That has not been done. However, I may say that when I vote on the second reading of the original bill, I am in fact voting for the amended bill even if it is not technically before the house, because that is the bill which will be discussed in committee.
The next point is this. The six months' hoist has been moved. That of course does not solve anything. It ignores what I think almost every hon. member has mentioned as a problem. It throws that problem into the waste-paper basket for six months. There is hardly a member who has spoken who does not admit that the situation is such that any government, no matter which government, must have certain powers to enable it to tide the economy of the country over the next six or twelve months, and to vote that the bill providing such powers be given the six months' hoist at this late hour in the session is to invite chaos. I certainly cannot vote for the six months' hoist. I am speaking of course for myself.
There are one or two things I should like to say. As I have just suggested, there are very few members who are willing to leave our unsolved problems without at least giving the government some opportunity to deal with them. That has been pretty well conceded. It has been suggested by one hon. member that the government has not the power anyway, that it never did have the power, that the government is being dictated to by some sinister, invisible force behind it. If that is so, then I think there is all the more reason

National Emergency
why this parliament should act. That hon. gentleman did not seem to be quite clear as to whether the government should go to those invisible and sinister forces and ask them for power or whether it should come to parliament for that power. In my opinion there are certain sinister powers in all nations which seek to influence governments. Those powers had pretty full sway in Canada after the last war, and they made a sorry mess of it. It is necessary that any government should have enough power to check that sinister force.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) in particular spoke of the very loyal opposition and the hon. member who preceded me in this debate spoke in a similar vein, as if every hon. member who happened to sit to the left of Mr. Speaker is, by virtue of that position on the floor of this house, in the official opposition. I do not so regard my position here. In all the years that I have been in parliament it is true that I have not had the good fortune to sit on the government side of the house.

I am not sure that I shall not be there before my hon. friend. If I am not it will be a bad thing for Canada.
Mr. ROSS (Souris)': The wish would not be father of the thought?

speechtext: I have never regarded my position here as that of a member of the loyal opposition. I regard myself as a representative of the people, free to measure every issue on its merits and to exercise my right as a member of parliament to vote on that measure whether it is moved by the leader of the official opposition or by any member of the government. In that connection I should like to read a passage from a speech of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, now Lord Bennett, delivered when he was Prime Minister of Canada. On that occasion, when he was addressing the house, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who was the leader of the opposition at that time-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Loyal, very loyal opposition! -had spoken in such a way as to indicate that all hon. members to the left of the Speaker were members of the opposition. The then Prime Minister said:
I was somewhat surprised at the ease with which he attached to his party all those who now sit to his left. He included them in those opposed to the government, but I had always believed that many of them gave to matters
brought before this parliament that measure of impartial consideration warranted by the merits of the proposals enacted.
I think that is a fair statement at least of the viewpoint which I hold with respect to the relationship of the group to which I belong to any measure which may be brought before this house, regardless of which party or group may move it.
I was surprised that the hon. member for Macleod who had discovered such a marvellous principle, and such a sacred one in this bill should not have been so attracted by this great principle which he had discovered that he would have known exactly how he was going to vote on the matter. But the principle, great though it appeared in his eyes, did not seem to have impressed him deeply enough to enable him to say whether he was going to vote for or against it. That does not seem to me to be a very great principle, but I noticed that he, like some others of his party, always manages to come back to the nest of his pet theory-there is an egg there, you know. He reminds me of a clucking hen who is trying to hatch out an infertile egg. While it cannot be hatched out, it can get bad. I think it has got quite bad.
Another hon. gentleman says that this bill is dangerous because it is going to give power, and power corrupts. He says that absolute power is absolute corruption. Well, Mr. Speaker, in that case the sooner this parliament gets rid of power the better. We do not want to be absolutely corrupted. If that were true I think we might well let the government have the power and it would get corrupted, and so badly corrupted that the official loyal opposition would become the government. It might be a good idea to do that. It is all nonsense to talk about power corrupting absolutely, because all the power which this parliament has to give comes from the people of Canada themselves. If they are going to be corrupted by power then just what are we doing aboutr-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen who talk like that should not be here, because they are exercising that portion of power which properly belongs to the riding which they represent.
I know that there are always dangers in delegating powers in our hands to governments and individuals, but if we do not do so here we are going to leave the problems in the hands of people who represent nobody but themselves and who have only their own bank accounts to think about. Although I am not a
National Emergency

Liberal, and vote against them nearly every time I get the chance, I would rather entrust power to the hands of a government which in one year from now can be thrown out because of what they may do with that power, than to leave that power blindly and stupidly in the hands of a profit-making bureaucracy, which is the most damnable kind of autocracy which ever existed in this or any other country.
I repeat that it is absolute nonsense to associate bureaucracy with a government organization when we know that the worst types of it exist in the very hearts of those organizations which do not wish any controls, which do not wish anything to stand between them and their so-called sacred rights of making profits.
All power comes from the people. The power is in our hands; I have a little bit of it because I represent the constituency of Cariboo. I recognize that in the terrific problems which now confront the people the government must have power to deal with them, and to the extent that I have the right to vote that little bit of power which has been entrusted to my care by my riding I vote that to a responsible and representative government. If that government misuses the power which I conceive it to be necessary for them to get, then I will be the first to kick them out for doing that, if I can. But they must have powers other than those ordinarily exercised by government in order to meet the situation now confronting the country. For that reason, sir, I shall vote for the amended
bill.

speechtext:
Ever since this bill came up for discussion we have had wishy-washy statements from time to time from the other side of the house. They have said that this is a

weak-kneed government. They also say, "Oh, yes, we want a little control, but we don't want this bill." In heaven's name let them get up and say what they do want, because it is my opinion that if we do not have this measure of control for at least a year there will be anarchy in this country. Let them get up and say that the farmers should not be assisted with subsidies, that the national labour code should be done away with, that regulation and regimentation regarding price control should all be abandoned. If that happens within the next year there will be anarchy, I say, that the poor people of this country will not be able to procure goods because the wealthy, which includes many of those who sit on the other side, will be getting nearly all. It is the voice of Toryism we are hearing to-day. Let them look to the last war and the years following it. When did the disaster of inflation overtake this country; was it during the war? No; the high prices, the inflation and all the other terrible things took place after the war. The Tories liked that, and so they want a repetition of it.
I am going to vote in favour of this bill because I want these regulations maintained for at least a little time. But let me say that if the first bill had been proceeded with I would have voted against it, and I am not just making this statement because the bill has been amended. All the opposition or suggestions did not come from the provincial premiers. There are men on this side who have the guts to speak out against the government; there are more of them here than I have witnessed in the opposition in my sixteen years in this house. I wish to refute now and in advance any suggestion that I am voting for this measure just out of weakness. I am going to vote for it because I think it is in the interests of the common people, in whose behalf I have not heard many voices raised from across the way.
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Mont-morency): Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to make a few comments in regard to the controls which are administered by the wartime prices and trade board under the Minister of Finance, who is in charge of the whole Canadian economy. I wish to make these few comments especially in connection with the production and distribution of goods and building materials. The controls were established to check and limit private enterprise in order to permit full production for necessary war purposes. Clearly, then, to my mind the removal of certain of these controls would stimulate an increase in production so as to take care of existing unemployment. It is not

National Emergency
possible right now for a citizen of this country who was not engaged in business or industry in 1941 to obtain quotas of materials or goods in order to set up a new industry or business. Therefore these controls have the immediate effect of protecting the monopolies and large industries which existed in 1941 and which are only too glad to eliminate any competition.
It is free enterprise which will develop production and increase employment in this country. The establishments of the armed forces and auxiliary services were increased to
784,000	during the war, while the various branches of industry concerned with national defence, but not including agricultural pursuits, provided work for 1,055,000 men and women. Therefore there were some 1,839,000 jobs, which number has been decreasing from day to day since the end of the war and most of which will be completely eliminated in the not far distant future. Such is the situation now that peace has been restored. Of course not all those who held the 1,839,000 jobs in our wartime economy will be laid off. The land, sea and air forces will not be completely demobilized, and it is likely that the peace-time establishments will be larger than they were in 1939. It is certain also that a large number of men who left farms, industries, businesses or financial institutions to join the armed forces or to work in war plants will return to their former positions, in which in many cases they were not replaced. When munitions plants closed down undoubtedly large numbers of women returned to their homes or to domestic service. Having regard to these circumstances, it is felt in official quarters that the creation of some 900,000 more jobs than existed in 1939 would offer a satisfactory solution of the unemployment problem. Further provisions have to be made each year to find jobs for about 60,000 young people who reach the age when they are expected to earn their own living. Naturally to attain this purpose the banks must make money available to industrial and business enterprises in order to create jobs. To my mind, inflation is used chiefly as an argument in favour of the continuation of certain of these controls. For my part, I believe the true and sole reason the government wishes to maintain control is to keep money in the banks in order to ensure more readily the success of their future loans, a motive which of course they will not admit; but the more we continue by this system of control to curtail production, the more unemployment will increase in the country. It is money that creates production and thereby prevents unemployment, and by controlling production or
limiting the distribution of goods produced to those who were in business in 1941, unemployment is deliberately brought about.
The government should free itself as rapidly as possible from those bureaucrats by whom it is surrounded. Of course it is necessary to retain certain controls. I believe that some should be kept for a short time to deal with the chaos resulting from the war. Without a doubt, if we defeat this bill it will mean the cancellation of all controls and throwing the whole economy of Canada into the hands of large cartels and trusts, to the detriment of the masses of the Canadian people. Further, now that the war is over, I believe it is urgent to hand back to the provinces the control over trade and industry of which they were deprived for war purposes. The prerogative of the provinces cannot be indefinitely trifled with, without touching off the spark which will destroy our national structure and will contribute more than anything else to the destruction of the unity which is essential to a country such as ours.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this bill is necessary, but with some limitation on its application; and I trust the government will apply its provisions in very few cases, and not beyond the one-year term set out in the bill.
(Translation): I have listened attentively to the speeches delivered by the hon. members for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) and for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon), and I have read, a few moments ago, the amendment whereby the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay moved that bill No. 15 be considered this day six months. I have heard the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay say that he was in favour of certain controls, that some of them should be maintained. I have also heard in this house a similar statement from the hon. member for Argenteuil and many other hon. members. Now, Mr. Speaker, if some controls are to be maintained, if some are necessary, how can we maintain them if we nullify bill No. 15 by our vote and our attitude? In voting against this bill, in giving it a six months' hoist, as proposed by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, we shall immediately plunge this country into chaos, an unavoidable consequence of the war policy that was followed and against which I always voiced the strongest opposition. This chaos now exists and it has resulted from the war. This chaos must be averted, and care must be taken not to hand over to the true dictators of this country the control of our national economy. The worst
National Emergency

dictatorship which we now have to face is the dictatorship of capitalists, of cartels, and of the Tories who sit in this house, because they are quite dangerous.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that controls cannot last indefinitely. But are we going to leave our whole economy in the hands of the people whose shadows haunt the lobbies of the House of Commons and who are bent on defeating bill No. 15? Are we going to let those who control finance in this country starve the common people by depriving them of their means of subsistence? That is what will happen if this bill is rejected.
I believe that any one who votes for this bill will show that he is imbued with sincere patriotism and is anxious to act the part of a true Canadian. It should not be thought that I am infavour of controls; on the contrary, I have always opposed them, but, in this case, we have to prevent our goods and our whole production from falling into the hands of powerful cartels, which want to crush the common people of this country.
There are to-day in my constituency many industrial centres where, owing to the existing controls, tenants can continue to pay the same rent as formerly; but for those controls the increase would have been exhorbitant. If such controls were left in the hands of some landlords, whose business principles are well known, they would at once evict from their houses a great number of the people of this country, or compel them to pay an exhorbitant rent. Those landlords would derive a great advantage from the present housing shortage.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if there are some controls which must remain, owing to the unusual conditions with which we are confronted, we should disregard partisanship and support the government's courageous policy which the honourable the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) did not hesitate to present in its true light.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members have listened with keen interest to the speeches in the debate thus far. It is a matter of personal regret to some of us that we could- not follow fully all that is said by some hon. members; but whether we can follow them or not, we give them credit for holding sincere views. We will read what they have said when the translations appear in Hansard, and consider them with every respect for those who have spoken.
I rise at this time to discuss two things. First, I should- like briefly to comment on the situation in which the house finds itself as a result of the introduction of bill No. 15, 
and the suggestion that in committee of the whole certain amendments will be made. I wish also to state, as briefly as I can, our position with respect to bill No. 15, to the amendments it is suggested will be proposed in committee, and to the general question as to the unusual powers, if any, the government should be given in the period of transition between the war and a more normal time of peace.
We have before us bill No. 15, which is known as the national emergency powers bill. It was introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) about two months ago, and the minister moved its second reading about two weeks ago. This is the bill upon which we are asked to vote. I am aware that as a result of certain criticism in the house, and perhaps also in the country, and in the , dominion-provincial conference which met a few days ago, the government has reconsidered the matter, and has made certain suggestions as to amendments that it is willing to have incorporated when the bill reaches the committee stage. I concede all that. The fact remains, however, that the bill upon which we are asked to vote is bill No. 15. It was introduced, as I said, two months ago and discussed by the Minister of Justice on second reading some two weeks ago.
To that bill, in its present form, we are entirely opposed. We are opposed to it for several reasons. We are opposed to it because of the unnecessary extent to which it invades the field of provincial jurisdiction. We are opposed to it because of the unnecessarily wide delegation of powers it confers upon the governor in council. We are opposed to it because of the wide powers the government seeks in connection with the entry of people into Canada, and the exclusion or deportation of people from Canada, and in connection with the question of the revocation of nationality. We are opposed to it because of the wholesale approval it requires us to give of the thousands of orders in council passed by the government under the War Measures Act, many of which we have never seen.
Having said that we are opposed to these wide powers as set out in the bill, let me say one thing more. We are not opposed to this government's having whatever powers are necessary to meet the emergent conditions of these post-war days. We are in favour of granting the government whatever powers are necessary to regulate prices, wage ceilings and the flow of essential goods in short supply.
I Personally, I am in favour of granting the government whatever other specific powers it can show to be necessary to meet the conditions ahead.

National Emergency
One hon. member, the member for Charle-voix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), has moved that the bill be given the six months' hoist. If carried, that motion would mean that the bill would be thrown aside and that no action would be taken. We could not support that failure to act. It would leave the government in the position of continuing the present War Measures Act. We take the position, Mr. Speaker, that the powers given in either act should be cut down and limited, and I am sure that members on all sides of the house agree with that view. But we are not in favour of taking away from the government all powers, nor are we in favour of leaving the government with excessive powers in its hands.
I think I have made our position clear. We are opposed to this bill as it stands, for the reasons I have given. The suggested amendments will no doubt be moved in committee of the whole, thus filtering down some of the objectionable features of the bill. But the amendments as now proposed do not remove the objectionable features. While we are opposed to the bill itself, and while we are opposed to giving it the six months' hoist, we think that in committee of the whole members on all sides of the house ought to come together to see how much we can further limit the autocratic powers which both this bill and its successor give, and yet enable the government to carry on and meet the problems of these days.
With all deference to the government, I think it has followed an entirely improper procedure. When the government reached the conclusion that important changes were so desirable in the bill as to warrant the printing of a new bill before the second reading of the original bill was proceeded with, they should have withdrawn the original bill completely and introduced a new one. That is the only course consistent with parliamentary procedure. As it is now, we are asked to support a bill to which members on all sides of the house are opposed. We are asked to support bill No. 15, the very bill which has been so severely censured in this house, and outside by the dominion-provincial conference, the very bill which the government itself is proposing to amend. Yet when we vote to-night, that is the bill we shall be voting on.
Bill No. 15 is, in our opinion, a most objectionable piece of legislation to be presented to this parliament. Should it ever become law in its present form, members of parliament might almost as well have packed their bags and started for home, because it would have clothed the government, in time of peace,, with full autocrat ic and dictatorial
power. This country would then be in the position of having an omnipotent government and an almost powerless and frustrated parliament.
It had been _our intention to oppose this bill with all the strength at our command. The fact that the government now proposes to amend it in considerable degree is highly complimentary to those members on all sides who have so strongly opposed certain sections of the bill, and it is the severest kind of criticism of the government by the government itself. The very fact that the government is proposing changes is an indication that considerable changes are necessary.
The general position of this party was placed before the house by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) a few days ago in a speech that many have admitted to be an able and complete statement, many portions of which have been approved by speakers on all sides of the house. Our criticisms of the bill were several in 'number. I shall refer now to only four of them, because there is no need to occupy the time of the house much longer since members wish, I am sure, to come to a decision on this matter.
Our first criticism is that the bill proposed a most serious invasion of provincial powers and gave reason to the provinces to fear ever-widening encroachments on their autonomy. The proposed amendments also in our judgment involve a substantial invasion of provincial jurisdiction, although less than in the original proposal. It is important that this house should know, before second reading is given, the extent to which the provincial premiers have approved the amendments proposed in this piece of paper that has been handed to us.
The second objection is the blanket and unlimited delegation of power to the governor in council. An example of this is to be found in the clause which enables the governor in council to make orders for the appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property. That is clause 3(l)(f). What a situation that would create-that a government in peace time should have the power to appropriate or forfeit property without due process of law!
Our third objection is to the pernicious clause which would enable the governor in council to make orders in respect of-I am now quoting from the bill-"entry into Canada, exclusion and deportation, and revocation of nationality." No clause more dangerous to national unity has ever found its way into a bill in this parliament. Hon. gentlemen opposite-and in this I agree with them-have made great political capital in
National Emergency

western Canada over the provisions of the Wartime Elections Act and the disenfranchisement which occurred therein of Canadians. I agree with that criticism, but this bill is subject to the same kind of criticism to an even greater degree in the form in which it is presented. So far as the official opposition is concerned we would resist to the limit the passage of that provision.
Our fourth objection is the wholesale approval and legalizing of all orders in council passed by the government under the War Measures Act during the last half dozen years. This parliament has never even seen some of those orders in council. Most members have seen very few of them, and some of the orders we know nothing at all about. Many of the orders in council passed under that legislation parliament knew nothing about, many have been tabled though all have not, and many we have never heard of; yet we are asked to legalize, and to approve all that has been done by the government under those thousands of orders in council during the last six years.
The government now indicates its willingness that some of these objectional clauses be removed from the bill. That is all to the good. But the fact remains that certain of the provisions which it proposes to retain, as well as certain of those which it proposes to substitute, are still of too sweeping a character. The particular powers which the government requires can be given in specific legislation if parliament is asked for them specifically. That would be much better than for a democratic assembly to give to any small group of men the sweeping powers sought, under this bill, even with its amendments.	.
In the five subclauses of the proposed section 2 many of the objectionable features are still retained by the sweeping language used. What the government proposes to do is to abandon the blanket delegation of authority proposed in this section of the bill and to redraft these specific clauses which were contained therein. But in redrafting these clauses the government still proposes to make them so wide in the authority conveyed that they are in effect almost as all-embracing as the blanket clause in section 3 of the bill before us.
Take, for example, paragraph (b) of section 2, subsection 1:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things ... as he may . . . deem necessary for . . .
(b) facilitating the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace.
(Mr. Bracken.]
This paragraph could not have been drafted in any broader or more sweeping terms. It conveys almost as unlimited power as section 3 of the bill before us. The fact is that no one with less wisdom than a Solomon or less ingenuity than a Philadelphia lawyer can define what limitation of power, if any, the paragraph actually contains.
Take another example in the same main section, paragraph (e) of the suggested amendments:
(e) continuing and discontinuing in an orderly manner, 'as the emergency permits, measures adopted during and by reason of the war.
This paragraph, read in conjunction with section 4 of the suggested changes gives the force of statute to all orders in council made under the War Measures Act, and permits the government, without the control of parliament, to continue in full force and effect the sweeping controls at present operating. [DOT]
What is the effect of all this? The effect is that we are asked to give parliamentary sanction-the full force of statute law-to all orders in council and to some orders in council which this parliament has never seen.
As I understand it, two classes of orders in council passed under the War Measures Act have not been laid before parliament:	First,
those orders in council the publication of which has been withheld for security reasons. In this category are included orders in council the publication of which is omitted or deferred under the authority of the secret documents (non-publication) order of 1941. Parliament does not know and has no means of knowing what orders in council may fall in this category. Second, there are some orders in council, even of an administrative nature, which have not been tabled. The government itself decides by itself what ones are of an administrative nature. There is nothing in the War Measures Act which requires this government to table these orders in council. Certain offers have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by the government to table them, and many of them have been tabled, but there is no obligation to table them, and in answers to questions and motions in this house it has been admitted that some of them have not been tabled. The house knows that certain ones have not been tabled until, by misadventure, they have come to light. We do not know and we have not been able to find out what orders in council in this category have not been laid before parliament. What we do know is that parliament is being asked to give the force of law to all these orders in council, known and unknown, some of which at least we have never seen..

National Emergency
Another objectionable feature, not of the same nature, as I have mentioned, I shall refer to.
A highly objectionable feature of the government's proposed amendments is the indefinite date of the termination of the measure. The government's new proposal provides that if parliament meets in November or December next the measure shall expire on the 31st day of December next, but it provides also that if parliament does not meet during November or December the measure shall only expire fifteen days after parliament first meets in 1947.
It is well known that the summoning of parliament is entirely within the control of the government. If they decide not to call parliament in November or December next year they can postpone the calling of it until at least the middle of April, 1947, at which time the government would be under the necessity of calling parliament in order to secure additional money to carry on. In those circumstances this bill would not expire until the end of April, 1947. The government and the government alone have the power to decide when parliament will be summoned, and they can postpone its summoning if they wish, in which case this bill would remain in . operation, as I have said, until April, 1947. In my opinion, this bill should not be operative for longer than a year, and the indefinit-ness and uncertainty of the present clause should be eliminated.
From what has been said in the debate, it is clear that the government has retreated from certain provisions of bill No. 15. They have not, however, eliminated all its objectionable features. This house has become accustomed this session to government retreats from established positions. One notable occasion was when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) withdrew the proposed tariff increases which were included in the budget resolutions.

speechtext: Before the section is carried, I have just a few remarks to make on one specific matter. I have great admiration for many of my new colleagues, who come from all over and who sit on all sides of the house, but some of them labour under handicaps. They can make the finest speeches; they can talk like angels, but their party will not benefit. I say that especially to my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party. Yesterday we had an illustration of this, and I refer to that in the best possible spirit. Of course there are many unfortunate occasions when we cannot maintain our friendships just because we are in public life, for the friendships that exist between men in private life cannot always be the same in public life. There are the old icons which have been hung on the wall of the council room of the Conservative party, Tory icons; and as long as they are kept there and worshipped, as long as there is a candle burning before them all the time, I do not see what results they can hope to achieve. In the party opposite are some very bright hon. gentlemen for whom I have the deepest admiration, who work hard and want to do something; but eventually they will come to the great divide, to the time when they will have to break the tie. They will reach the cross-roads and realize that the earth is turning and that those who have inherited power and might from others who have been elected by the people, as well as those who have never succeeded in getting elected by the people, should be completely discarded. There is another class of individual who must be discarded as well. It includes those who never took the risk of running in a riding. They are in a class by themselves. I will not classify them as birds of prey; I name no one, but there are two main categories, those whom the people did not want and those whom the people would not want if they went before the people. I will tell the committee the story of an experience I had in January, 1942, and of the result which was achieved in February of that year. Here in the house I objected to the person who was running in York South as a Progressive-at least as a Conservative, and I do not know what the qualifying word was.

I did so in a cold-blooded way in order to express my deep regret and sorrow that the magnificent parliamentary efforts of some bright men were handicapped precisely on account of the fact that they did not throw these Jonahs overboard and did not keep themselves distinct from those people who had outlived their usefulness, if they ever had any. The leader of the C.C.F. party and the Minister of Agriculture were very cruel in using the ad hominem argument, which could not have been used against those honourable and bright colleagues if they had broken the tie and left in the ditch the glorious icons of the past, which do not get a single vote for anyone in this chamber who represents the Progressive Conservative party.
