I thank you. I tell the committee only this. It was only yesterday that both the leader of the C.C.F. and the Minister of Agriculture made excellent

National Emergency
speeches by using ad hominem arguments against the brightest debaters in the new generation of the Progressive Conservative i parly. Their speeches were remarkable-on both sides.
But what I am giving now is some friendly advice to those colleagues whom I admire in order that in future nobody may use ad hominem arguments against them by quoting what Arthur Meighen. R. B. Bennett, or anybody else who has been discarded by the people as leader of the Conservative party, might have said. That is my point. It is just in order to be helpful that I say this. Moreover, I shall be thankful to them if they will reciprocate by offering their own suggestions or advice, and I shall take those suggestions or advice in the best possible spirit. Perhaps there may be some occasion when they might do so, and I hope they will.
I believe I can say in a sentence or two what I dislike in the bill. I am opposed to these controls. We may try to do something to prevent future evils, but perhaps we shall have to do so in a different way, and it is my hope that at the next session of parliament a committee will be formed of hon. members belonging to all groups who will see if we in this chamber cannot find a solution to prevent future trouble.
I am definitely and categorically opposed to approval by this chamber of orders in council. The government has its responsibility in that regard; we have none. As a member of parliament I am not prepared to assume responsibility for orders in council passed by all controllers, and we are not going to ratify that sort of thing. I cannot ratify by my vote orders in council which I reprove in my mind. I hope I have, made myself clear, and if I have not I am ready to answer any questions.

Mr. Chairman, I regret very much to have to continue with my question of privilege. I was interrupted at six o'clock, and I cannot leave it at that. While we were discussing bill No. 15 in committee I read a telegram which bears the signature of Mr. Arthur Meighen, dated November 30, 1917, and afterwards the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) rose and used language to which I am not accustomed. I took some notes when he spoke, and in part, he said this:
At least the ordinary proprieties should be observed in connection with outstanding Cana-_ dians, that we do not malign them by state' ments which must to the knowledge of the person reading them be untrue.
Meaning by that, that what I had said was a lie. The hon. member went pretty far, and I say that for two reasons. In the first, place, the telegram was read in the house on January 30, 1942, as appears at page 179 of Hansard, and when it was read one of the deans of the house, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), said:
It is on Hansard.
He meant by that, that when I read the telegram it had appeared on Hansard previously and that that was where I got it from.
There is another matter that is beyond me, namely that on that occasion, on January 30, 1942, the hon. member of the opposition who spoke immediately after me did not lodge a protest similar to the one that he made around six o'clock to-day. The only thing that he said, in reply to the reading of this telegram and another one that I shall read afterwards, both of which are in Hansard, was this:
Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Lake Centre): As I listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) it came to me once more what
'Mr. Pouliot.]
democracy in this empire and this country means: That in the midst of war, when all of us are worried and concerned, an hon. member may rise in his place and make the type of speech he made to-day. That is freedom of speech-the opportunity to express one's view in parliament.
The only sentence that he added to that was this:
I .am not going to endeavour to follow the hon. member m what he has said.
If the telegram was denied by the man whose name appeared at the bottom of it in Hansard, how is it that the hon. member did not protest two years ago? How can he remember now a thing he never thought of two years ago? Then afterwards he used abusive language with regard to an hon. member of the House of Commons who tries to act as a life-saver for himself and his party.
That being done, sir, I have just one word to add to the discussion that is now before the Chair. It is that the question of freedom and the question of the rights of parliament are both matters of tremendous magnitude, and no member of parliament can disregard those vital questions.

Those who say "hear, hear" will have first to hear, hear, because something has to be told to them.
There are precedents which are good and which must be followed, but there are others which are bad and which cannot be followed by a body composed of men who are supposed to be the defenders of freedom, not only their own but that of others also, and for all mankind if possible. The greatest encroachment that was made on the liberty of man in Canada was made by a parliamentarian some years ago, and that precedent must never be followed in the future. I hope that no government, whatever it may be, will ever dare to imitate the action of that person. Here is the text of a document which appears in Hansard of January 30, 1942, and which reminds me of Nero, Diocletian and all the persecutors of the past. That document scandalized me the first time I heard of it, so much so that I never thought a man living in a democratic country could do a thing like that. That is at page 199 of Hansard of January 30, 1942. What was written then surpasses what Nero and Diocletian ever dreamed of, or Hitler, or Mussolini-all of them. It was dated June 17, 1919, and it was a telegram from Mr. Arthur Meighen to Mr. Andrew. Listen to it:
Notwithstanding any doubt I have as to the technical legality of the arrest and detention at Stony Mountain (penitentiary) I feel that

National Emergency
rapid deportation is the best course now that the arrests are made, and later we can consider rectification.
The hon. member for Lake Centre will be well advised to drop the icon of Arthur Meighen on the floor and break it, for the sake of his party and for his own sake.

speechtext:
I have read over
the amendments and compared them with the original section which is to be amended, and with the exception of one or two subsections, I submit that this new section incorporates all the objected items to which I made reference when I spoke on the introduction of the bill. The only objected item which has been removed is "entry in Canada, exclusion and deportation, and revocation of nationality," a section which was nefarious in concept and would have resulted in untold hardship to Canadian citizens. That subsection has been removed. Then, too, the government has seen fit to follow one suggestion which was made, namely, that all orders in council passed under this act should be laid on the table of parliament, giving this house an opportunity of annulment within a reasonable period. But subsection 3 of section 2 does not remove the major objection that we on this side of the house took to the original bill, because in section 4 provision is made that:
The orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act or pursuant to authority created under the said act in force immediately before the day this act comes into force shall, while this act is in force, continue in full force and effect subject to amendment or revocation under this act.
In other words, no provision is made whereby parliament will be placed in a position that it may annul orders in council which were passed during the period of the war under the War Measures Act. The only power which is given to parliament is the power to annul orders in council passed on and after the date this measure comes into effect. Our major objection to this bill in so far as the order in council feature is concerned in general was that parliament was being asked to approve all the multitude of orders in council passed during the period of war, without knowledge of their contents, in many cases without those orders in council having been brought before parliament. The only provision now, under section 4, is for amendment or revocation, but not for annulment within the meaning of section 2, annulment being an act of parliament in consequence of the machinery being set in operation by a member of this house; amendment or revocation, an act which only the governor in council * may follow. We on this side of the house intend to press to have every order in council which was passed during the period of the war under the War Measures Act laid on the table of the house, giving to hon. members an opportunity to repudiate those which ought to be repudiated.
I come now to the sections. A few days after the opening debate the dominion-provincial conference met in the city of Ottawa. Many felt that the premiers and attorneys-general of the provinces had been consulted and that as a result of the consultation a new bill had been prepared in place of the old. To-day, however, the Minister of Justice quite frankly states that such is not the fact, that all that took place was a discussion, that notes were taken of the discussion, and that in certain cases the suggestions of the provincial representatives were accepted.
These sections as now constituted actually embody, with the exception of the one dealing with naturalization, all the subsections that were objected to by us on this side of the house. For instance, we raised strong objection to controls over production, manufacture, trading, exportation and importation. It was pointed out that with that power in the hands of the governor in council the government placed itself in the position of being able to control all the business in this country. That subsection has been removed and in place of it has been substituted another section 2, 1 (b), providing for measures necessary for facilitating the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace. The only difference between that subsection and the new one is that new words have been used which no doubt it was believed would be more palatable than those that appeared in the original bill.
Again, we raised strong objection to the governor in council having power to take control over transportation by air, road, rail and water. There has never been an explanation by the minister why the government needs this power. Why does the government wish to take
National Emergency

control over transportation by road or by air, or water or rail? What is the purpose? The subsection was removed, but when you look into the amendment you find that it is hidden away in another section, in section 2 (c) which gives the government the same power it would have had under the original bill; for it provides that the governor in council shall have power to maintain, control and regulate supplies and services, prices and transportation. In other words, it was taken out of one subsection and placed in another with the identical powers remaining in the governor in council.
We raised strong objection, to the power which the government was asking for of appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property. We asked what the purpose of the government was in seeking power to forfeit in 1945, forfeiture meaning the taking over of land or personal property without compensation. That subsection has been removed and in place of it another has been brought in namely 2, 1, (c), which in different terms and terminology still grants the absolute power the governor in council had asked for under the original bill.
To the original bill have been added certain other powers. Section 2 1(a) provides for maintaining the armed forces of Canada during occupation of enemy territory, demobilization, and providing for rehabilitation of the members thereof. That was not in the old bill. I feel that' is necessary, because we are endeavouring to get the session over and there would be various matters in connection with veterans affairs which until the next parliament meets would have to be dealt with by order in council.
There is another subsection which grants the widest powers possible to the governor in council. It assists relief of suffering and the restoration and distribution of essential supplies and services in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in foreign countries that are in grave distress as a result of the war. Power is now asked for greater than was sought in the first bill, whereby the governor in council will be empowered under a blank cheque to do anything that he feels is necessary anywhere in the world so long as he considers that it is to relieve grave distress as a result of the war.
When the government agreed to amend the original bill many of us felt that the amendments which it had in mind, having regard to press dispatches in advance, would actually remove the causes of objections that we were raising; but anyone reading these amendments must come to one conclusion only, and that is that the government, having to recede in

face of public objection, in face of objections raised in the house, in face of objections raised in the dominion-provincial conference, decided, instead of withdrawing the bill, to introduce a new one with as wide powers, except in the two instances I have mentioned, as were granted before, the only change being one of terminology.
But they did something else. They gave the bill a new face; they added the word "transitional". They found themselves in the position of having to save face, after having introduced a bill that shocked the sensibilities of the people of the dominion; and having found themselves in that position they followed the course of face-lifting, altering the face of the bill as it was originally. But the same tell-tale wrinkles are there, the same wrinkles that spell dictatorship in this country if we do not oppose the granting of these powers to the government. All that has been done, with the exception of the removal of the two subsections to which I have referred, is to reshuffle the deck, leaving in it the same cards but placing them in different positions and numbering them differently as compared with the old bill.
I think we have a right to ask at this time certain pertinent questions of the government, and the first is this: Are we not entitled to a complete summary of the degree to which war controls have been removed to date? Are we not entitled to know to what extent these powers are to be used as anticipated at the present time? Are we not entitled to know to what extent price controls are to be continued and to what extent they are to be removed, as they are being removed to-day in the United States? Are we not entitled to know now, before granting this power to the governor in council, the extent to which wages are to be maintained at their present level?
Are we not entitled to know the plans of the governor in council in reference to labour? Does the governor in council intend to continue the measures which were passed during the period of the war? Is selective service to be continued in its present form? To what extent are there to be releases from some of the controls which to-day are unfair to labour? We have a right to know these things before we place in the hands of the governor in council the powers for which he asks.
We can only rehabilitate this country if we restore to the small man the opportunity of going into business. It is true that during the last year some of the controls over a man going into a new business have been removed. Possibly they have all been removed; but the situation is this: while a man may open

National Emergency
business he cannot get supplies. All he receives from the wartime prices and trade board is a hunting licence enabling him to go hunting for supplies. But those supplies are denied him and the opportunity to go into business is denied him.
Under these powers to what extent does the government intend to assure that retailers shall v receive their fair and just share of the goods which are available? What is the situation with regard to clothing, woollens, footwear and the like? To what extent does the government intend to impose still greater controls with a view to assuring a fair and proper distribution of scarce 'materials? I believe we have a right to have an answer to these juestions at this time.
I point out this fact, while we in Canada ire asked to give the governor in council those tremendous powers, a change is taking place in the United States because of the fear of deflation. The Secretary of Commerce, Henry Wallace, said recently:
Higher wage rates must be given labour to cushion loss of the war's overtime and incentive take-home pay.	*
They have taken steps in that direction. The trades and labour congress has gone on record in Great Britain that controls on labour should be speedily relaxed. They say:
The congress recommendation is that workers over thirty be exempted from controls altogether and permitted to leave even essential industries in order to look for permanent peace-time employment. The congress officials feel that controls exercised against the will of the men are in fact a hindrance rather than a help to the food output, and that men would work much more willingly if allowed to choose their own jobs. I believe that the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour should explain these matters at this time for the benefit of the house and the country.
While we have received haphazard explanations from time to time from one minister and another, we have not yet found the over-all picture. I therefore ask the ministers and the government to answer these questions: What are your immediate present plans to maintain the purchasing power and the scale of expanding production capacity? What measures are being taken by the government now to do what the government of the United States is doing, namely, to combat possible deflation? Much has been said about inflation after the last war. There was inflation until 1921, which was followed by a serious period of deflation. The government must have plans to forestall deflation, and they should be made available to the house at this time.
In this connection may I say, sir, that a special committee of the United States house of representatives investigated federal agencies during the month of November. They brought down a report which I think is applicable to Canada at this time. In part that report read as follows:
The policy of adherence to rigid formulae has retarded reconversion, prevented production, especially in low-priced commodities, has restricted opportunity for full employment . . . It has compelled manufacturers to discontinue and abandon production of pre-war low-priced commodities they were skilled in making in great volume, and has permitted newcomers to manufacture such commodities at higher prices than were necessary to enable those already in the field to stay in business.
These words of the committee of the United States house of representatives may well apply to Canada, having regard to the similarity of our economic conditions.
We have [DOT] continued to preach the dangers of inflation, and I am not arguing that at the moment, i We have talked about the necessity of maintaining wage schedules at the present level, and of preserving price schedules; whereas in United States the President said in his speech in late October:
Wages must be allowed to be increased.
He indicated that higher wages are as vital to business and agriculture as to labour; for consumers cannot buy the products of industry and the farms unless they earn sufficient wages. He then used these words:
I am convinced we must get away as quickly as possible from government controls and get back to the free operation of our competitive system.
The United States is extending; it is not decontrolling unnecessarily fast, but it is working in that direction as speedily as possible, and toward the removal in part and in whole of some of those controls. I therefore ask that at this time the government give to the house and the country a full, complete and integrated statement of government plans; a statement as to the use it intends to make of the powers which parliament is being asked to give, to the end that we shall not be in the position of being asked to place our parliamentary rights ip pawn without realizing the security which the government is giving in return for these rights.
I have not received an answer to the suggestion that I made. We all want to cooperate in this matter.

speechtext:
Hon. members laugh because they have never learned the meaning of that. We are seriously endeavouring to
National Emergency

assist in this tremendous problem. I regard my hon. friends' sincerity most highly, and in return I ask the same consideration in a matter such as this, which concerns the future of this country. I know that all hon. members are anxious to get away, but we realize we are faced with a problem which is greater than anything we shall have to face at an}' time in the years to come. I again make the plea I made the other day. There are men in this house who have made a great success of their business; there are men who understand the ramifications of finance; there are men who are representative of labour and of agriculture. Let us take this bill and place it before a committee composed of such men. They can hear evidence, listen to the story of the controllers and ascertain from them exactly what they intend to do, and why they need those powers. As a result of securing that evidence we shall be in a position where we can intelligently discuss this problem.
The extradition bill was sent to a committee. That is an important bill, impinging as it does upon the rights and the liberties of Canadians, but in my opinion it is no more important-in fact it is less important-than this bill which concerns the welfare and the future of every man and woman in Canada. Why not give us three or four days in committee? Give us an opportunity of having those men before us. Let us ascertain from them why they made certain orders. Let us ascertain from the rentals controller why rentals controls are applied in certain villages where there is no shortage of houses whatsoever. Let us ascertain why it has been applied in certain other ways resulting even in petty tyranny. Let us see the picture. Let us endeavour to work together for one purpose, so that when we delegate these powers to the governor in council they will be utilized for the welfare of this country, which comes first and foremost. In all sincerity I make that appeal. We have an opportunity to make a tremendous contribution in that way, an opportunity to assure that parliament will have been supreme, so that instead of blindly placing these tremendous powers in the hands of controllers and the like, parliament will know why they have been placed there and how they are intended to be used during the next two or three months.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Well, Mr. Chairman, we have been hearing some pretty extraordinary things for the last couple of days, and one of the most extraordinary is to hear them called "cooperation". I have been listening attentively to all that has been said in this

debate, and I have yet to learn whether or not the official opposition wants a 'bill passed. I will make an exception as to the very objective speech made this afternoon by the leader of the opposition. The hon. member who has just sat down says that the tell-tale wrinkles are still there. That is true; the tell-tale wrinkles are still there. We heard some extraordinary statements about this bill yesterday afternoon and yesterday evening. When we continued the debate this morning we seemed to be getting back on another plane, but we did not stay there very long. The tell-tale wrinkles are always there.
Some hon. members have made it quite clear that they do not want controls. The hon. member for Stanstead wound up his speech by saying that what this country needed was a government with nerve enough to take off the controls. Most of the other hon. members disagreed with that stand. One can understand a position of that kind. The hon. gentleman was supported by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains and by other hon. members. They are concerned with* the effect of these controls upon the owners of property and the exceptional opportunities owners of property are losing at this time because the controls are in existence. One can understand something of that kind. The hon. member says; Of course we are told there are dangers. Prices went up after the last war, and they would go up again after this war; but what of it? The price of sugar would rise from five cents to twenty-five cents. The price of butter would go from thirty-seven cents to sixty cents; but what of it? Shall that weigh against the loss of freedom that is entailed in the maintenance of these controls? In July, 1914, flour sold for $3.30. In the spring of 1920 it sold for $8.40. Sugar sold for $5.50 per 100 pounds in 1914; in 1920 it was $25. Butter was thirty cents a pound in 1914; in 1920 it was eighty-seven cents; but what of it? How does that weigh in the balance? Bacon was 254 cents a pound in 1914; in the spring of 1920 it was sixty cents. In 1914 milk was 84 cents a quart; in 1920 it was 154 cents. Coffee was thirty-seven cents in 1914 and sixty-two cents in 1920. Eggs went from twenty-seven cents a dozen in 1914 to eighty-eight cents a dozen in 1920; potatoes went from twenty-five cents a peck to $1.08 and fresh pork from twenty cents to forty-two cents.
Well, what about it? To some, perhaps nothing about it; but to this government it is a matter of considerable concern, and this government feels that it has behind it not only a majority in this house but a majority in this country. This government has not the nerve to take off controls and make oppor-

National Emergency
tunities for those who would derive benefit from those opportunities at the expense of the mass of the population. This government has not that nerve. If there are people in the country who want a government with that nerve, let them choose it from the other side of the house. When I proposed the second reading of this bill I said in so many words that whenever a government had to ask for powers of this kind it was always an opportunity for whatever party was in opposition to assert its attachment to constitutional and traditional rights, and to try to make out that the other party was departing from them. But I did not expect that it would go the lengths it has gone in this debate, and especially I did not expect that it would come with such violence from those who had supported and passed the legislation to which the leader of the C.C.F. party referred last evening and which is in the statutes of 1931.
It is regrettable that the circumstances are such that controls are required; but they are required, and this government has the nerve to come to the country and say it intends to see that they are maintained as long as they are required. La ligue des proprietaires, no doubt very respectable people, object to this bill because they are not allowed to use their property as they see fit and to get the better returns they mention in the representations they submit to members of parliament. Their position is much to be deplored, but there is a serious shortage of housing for the Canadian population at the present time, and that shortage would make for unduly enhanced rentals if there were not rental controls.
. Hon. members say that we are asking for extraordinary powers and for a blank cheque. How many days ago was it that this house passed, for the sixth or seventh time, an appropriation this time of $1,365,000,000, unanimously and without a word of dissent from the hon. member for Eglinton or any other hon. member on the other side of the house? Second reading of that bill was unanimously approved in this house on November 22; I need not refer to the page of Hansard. What are the terms of that bill, which hon. members quite rightly found it appropriate to pass because the country is not yet in a normal situation? The terms, which are identical in each of these bills since 1939, were these:
From and out of the consolidated revenue fund there may he paid and applied, beyond the ordinary grants of parliament, a sum not exceeding one billion, three hundred and sixty-five million dollars less the amount provided for by the War Expenditure and Demobilization Appropriation Apt, No, 1, 1945, subject to allotment by treasury board, towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the
authority of the governor in council during the year ending the thirty-first day of March, 1946, for;
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.
How wide is that; how broad is. that? Then:
(b)	The conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	the expeditious demobilization of the
Canadian armed forces;	[DOT]
(d)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever-

Surely it is not the leader of the opposition. When I spoke about something similar a few weeks ago I was quoting from a speech he delivered on April 23, 1945, I believe it was, in which he said that of course no one could contest the necessity for having applied these controls during the war, and that they could not be expected to come off in one fell swoop after the war was over. Someone asked the other night: What would be the impression of a traveller who would return to parliament from Mars after a stay there of fifteen or twenty, years? One would

almost think there were lots of those travellers in this house. They do not seem to have been anywhere near this country for the last several months.

speechtext:
Terrible.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: My hon. friend says that it is terrible. Has my hon. friend found no one who did not find there were conditons which unfortunately were terrible for him and which it was not possible to alleviate immediately? Does my hon. friend know of no one who is not in a position to find convenient and proper shelter in this country? Does the hon. member realize that everything possible since V-E day has been done to provide shelter? When I hear hon. members saying that if there was a shortage of housing it was because there had not been proper foresight, prudent looking ahead, I ask: Is there any hon. member who would, while the war was on, have wished the man-power or the resources of this country to be diverted to the building of houses instead of being devoted to fighting the enemy? If there is, I would . like to see him rise in his place in this house and say so and take the responsibility for that attitude before his countrymen.
There were many things said in the speech delivered by the hon. member for Stanstead yesterday afternoon. No one on this side would have ventured to go so far as he did in the praise he meted out to the government for what was done. Here is what he said at page 2921 of Hansard:
I do not criticize those who had the responsibility of enacting the legislation that brought these controls about. They were anxious to win the war. They had but one aim in view, and they have achieved that aim.
I would fully subscribe to that. The Canadian people had one aim, namely to win the war, and the Canadian people achieved that aim. So long as it was necessary to do that, they had but one thought in mind-win the war, and do the things necessary to win the war-and they were not thinking of slum clearance and of building houses at that time. But immediately V-E day came, the effort was 47696-189J
made to remedy the lack of housing and to overcome the inactivity in that field which the war had compelled for several years. It has been stated in this house that the target is the construction of 50,000 new homes within the space of a calendar year, and that target will be realized. But even with that, there is still a terrible housing situation, and there is still a situation which, if rental controls were removed, would give la Ligue des proprietaires handsome returns on their ownership of rental houses. It is necessary, most hon. members are agreed, to maintain some controls.
But some hon. members say:	Give us a
clear-cut plan. Tell us what were the orders in council that were made during the war period, what are those that are still in operation, what are those that you want to continue in operation, what are those that you are going to repeal, and so forth? That is very nice. There were almost, it was said, one hundred thousand orders in council and treasury minutes passed during the war. The clerk of the privy council has given me exact figures about that. I have read the terms of one of the war appropriation bills, and they were all in the same terms. Practically all the administrative orders might have been made under the terms of these appropriation bills. But at that time, rightly or wrongly, our whole thoughts were on winning the war, and there was in operation the War Measures Act, which had been passed in 1914 by a previous government of another complexion. That act was very broad in its terms and was sufficient authority for anything that the government felt it was reasonable and proper to do toward winning the war. For that reason the War Measures Act was in a very large number of cases expressly referred to in orders in council that would have been fully justified under other measures. There was a small number, practically less th an 3 per cent, of orders of a legislative nature. Hon. members have said that they did not know what those were; they never saw them. Well, if they did not know them, if they never saw them, it is because they did not take the trouble-it was a considerable trouble and I am not blaming them because I did not do it myself-of going over these six or eight volumes of war proclamations and orders that were put out as blue books and then the four volumes per annum, too, of Canadian war orders and regulations, four published each year with a .cumulative explanatory index every three months showing the effect of each upon the other.
Naii/mal Emergency

* It,is true: that we did not do that neatly as iit was done in the United Kingdom. I have begone me the 16th edition of the defence regulations. Evidently fifteen times prior to the 9th of May, 1945, they consolidated them and issued them in book form, numbered seriatim-a very convenient thing. The lawyers in the United Kingdom were in a more comfortable position to find out what the regulations were than were the lawyers in Canada, but there are not very many lawyers in Canada who have seriously complained of the fact that up to V-E day the government of Canada and the people of Canada were giving their whole thought to winning the war, and not to tidiness in the form * in which the regulations had -to be issued. I am not in a position to say to the hon. member for Lake Centre that this is the Series of orders in council that are in force and that would remain enforced under the proposed section 4 of this bill. I have been doing other things than compiling these orders for the purpose of giving that information to the hon. member, and I am not sorry that I did other things. I think the things I did were more important than would have- been the compiling of these orders to give the hon. member that information.
What this bill seeks to do now is to put, in a form which we think is apt to be more acceptable to some hon. members than was the previous form, an enumeration of the powers which it may be necessary to exercise. I hope it will not be necessary. I hope that from now on it will be possible to get along without exercising any of those powers for other purposes than for cutting down restrictions. But I am not in a position to guarantee that we are going to get through the next few months and maintain an orderly system of such controls as are necessary and an orderly decontrol without ever doing something new. I am not prepared to guarantee that that can be accomplished, and therefore I took the advice of the law officers as to the form a bill should have to make it possible to meet such unforeseen conditions as may arise in that process.
Much has been made of the terms of some of the subsections of bill No. 15, for instance section 2 (b):
facilitating the readjustment of industry and commerce to the requirements of the community in time of peace.
I am not much concerned whether that stays *there or not.

speechtext:
To bring in
socialism.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If there is never any more socialism in Canada than this country will get from this government under this bill, the hon. member may remain perfectly undisturbed. The clause is in exactly the same form in section 1, paragraph (c) of this supplies and services (transitional powers) act. Quite frankly, it might be invoked, but I do not think it will be. I do not at the present moment see very well how it could be, but I am told that it might be of some use in doing something to the foreign exchange control regulations which are in existence and which the government intend to ask parliament to continue in existence under this bill. *
Then, the hon. member for Lake Centre said that there were many of these clauses which in other words would express power to which he had taken exception on November 23. I do not deny that. We are not trying to meet all the objections which the hon. member raised on the 23rd of November. It is not only for the sake of the hon. member for Lake Centre that we are asking that this legislation be passed; we are asking that it be passed for the people of Canada. In determining what we would retain in the bill we were much more concerned with what would be in the interests of the people of Canada than with what would meet the objections of the hon. member for Lake Centre.
The hon. member says that no one has suggested why in the former bill there was some reference to transportation by air, by rail, by water or by road. Did the hon. member never get any complaint from anyone about the restrictions to which he was subjected in the use of automobiles, or autobuses, or trucks on the highways because of the-at the time-deplorable shortage of rubber for tires, and of oil and gasoline, for motive power? Fortunately most of these restrictions have now been removed, but there are still in force a number of restrictions on travel by rail. Every time a shipload of returned men arrives at one of the ports of eastern Canada there is a general mobilization of rail equipment which is regulated and controlled in the interest, not only of the men who are returning, but in the interest of Canada, because Canada owes those men the best transportation it can provide for them when it is bringing them

National Emergency
home from the fields where they went and risked their lives for the institutions of this Canada of theirs.
These powers are expressed in language which is broad and which is intended to be broad. It is intended to meet contingencies which may arise. But, so that we would follow" another example set by that socialist government of the United Kingdom, we put into this bill a provision that anything the governor in council chose to do under it would be done upon the assumption that if it were to be done by legislation it w'ould have the consent of the Senate and of the House of Commons as well as of the crown. Legislation, to be enacted, requires the three branches of parliament. Under these special conditions we think that, for the sake of having expeditious action, it is proper that the governor in council have from the Senate and the House of Commons a delegation of power to be exercised on the assumption that whatever the governor in council does thereby has the implied consent of the Senate and the House of Commons; and we say that we shall bring down everything which is thus done at the earliest possible moment and lay it on the tables of parliament, and that if either house chooses to say by resolution that it should not continue in operation, thereupon it shall cease to operate. Does any hon. member think that the governor in council, the government advising His Excellency the Governor General, will take the risk lightly of putting through things which it will bring before this parliament and which this parliament will then resolve to annul?	.
Let us get down to earth. I think most hon. members want the situation that is going to unroll itself during the next several months to be properly taken care of; and any government which exercises these powers in view of the fact that it will immediately declare to both houses of parliament how it exercises them and for what purpose it exercises them, will be reasonably careful that it does not indulge in fancies which will be frowned upon by either house.
I have heard the question asked, why leave it to either house thus to annul something decided by the governor in council. Quite frankly that was put in there to safeguard the absolute right of this house, unfettered in any way, to disapprove anything that the governor in council might do. If members of this house prefer to have it that a resolution of both houses of parliament will be required to have the effect of annulling something decided by the governor in council, I know there are a great many on this side who will be far better pleased with it; and if, when we are
discussing that provision, ' it appears ' to be the desire^ of this house to subject its decision to a concurring decision from the other place, there will be no objection from the government to accepting a suggestion of that kind. But it was felt that it would not be respecting the full power and control of this house to have it otherwise than as expressed in the bill.
The section that is now under consideration provides, as the hon. member for Lake Centre so well pointed out, that the governor in council may do anything that he deems necessary or advisable because of the national emergency arising out of the war for any of the purposes enumerated in the five subparagraphs. The limitation is not on the objects which- the orders in council or regulations may deal with, but on the purposes for which he may deal with them. He may deal with them for any one of the purposes thus enumerated. Subsection 2 provides that the orders shall, for" the purpose of the Interpretation Act, be deemed to be regulations. That is merely for the purpose of avoiding having to repeat in this bill what is contained in the Interpretation Act, which applies to all enactments and which is a statute of some forty-two sections.	*
^ The third subsection provides that the orders shall be laid before parliament and that there shall be a period of twenty-eight days during which, in either house, a resolution may be moved to annul; and once more, if such a resolution is moved, the government will do its best to bring it to a decision at once, because it has no fear that the kind of things it will pass will not have the approval of the majority in this house, whatever may be the views of those who challenge the order in the resolution tabled. VThe government will have this further incentive to getting prompt decision upon it, that the psychological effect of these regulations on the Canadian public is now very satisfactory and has been built up over a period of several years; and if there were anything happening now to make those who are disposed to evade the provisions of the regulations feel that there had been any loosening up, it would be a considerable task to recreate by enforcement action the psychol-, ogy which is necessary if we are to have the whole of the public respect the regulations that are made in the interests of all. That is all there is in section 2.
I am not in a position to answer specific questions put to me by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I am not in a position to say which control will come off or when. I can say to the hon. member that this morning's papers announced the removal of controls on
National Emergency

construction permits. Of course that does not mean that it will be possible to build any more constructions than the material available will provide for, but it does mean that no one will have to get any other permit than the permits from the local authorities, to proceed when he can with any construction he chooses to undertake.
The hon. member said that he was not sure whether there were still permits in regard to the starting of new businesses. Personally I do not know; perhaps the Minister of Finance knows. But certainly there has been no removal of the quota system on the distribution of much of the material used in industry. There is still a shortage of that material. There was established and there is still being maintained a quota system whereby in many cases about eighty per cent of the material available is distributed on the quotas established during the period of 1941. There is about twenty per cent that is free for distribution to others than holders of quotas. Is that a good thing? Is it a bad thing? It is a thing which worked out very satisfactorily during the war. It is a thing which we think is good and which we are going to take the responsibility of maintaining because we think it is good so long as the reasons for it are apparent.
The hon. member asks whether price controls are to be removed. Price controls will certainly not be removed in the immediate future. Are wage ceilings to be done away with? Wage ceilings will certainly not be done away with in the immediate future. Is there to be any modification in those matters? That has been and is and will continue to be daily under active consideration for the purpose and to the end of lightening and removing these controls just as rapidly as the government feels that they can be removed and that it will still be respecting its responsibility to the Canadian public.
Reference has been made to what has been happening in the United States. It is not the place here to criticize what is happening there. I will make no comment. I will ask those hon. members who have had occasion to visit in the United States recently whether ,what is going on there is better suited to the needs of the majority of the public than what is happening here. I think I will leave it at that. We may be wrong, but we think that the manner in which the situation has been handled here has been more satisfactory to the Canadian public than had we duplicated here what has happened in the country of our very good neighbours to the south, and we intend to continue to apply the policy which we, with our advisers, consider is best

suited to the needs of the Canadian people. If we have to make any new regulations we shall bring them here, and we shall get the opinion of the members of this house upon them.	.
As to those which are now in effect, if this house accepts, as I hope it will, the bill with the proposed amendments that we have suggested here and maintains in effect-I do not care whether it be by virtue of the law or whether they say to us the governor in council may continue in force under this measure all the things in force on the day when it comes into operation-the regulations we shall be satisfied. We are not trying to get rid of any responsibility. We do not feel the burden of any responsibility is too great for us to carry. We carried it through the month of June and we are prepared to carry it forward to any other contest when it may have to be judged by the public. We are not asking anyone else to take any portion of it, and we are not prepared to give any of those who criticize it any part of the credit which gave us the result which was achieved at the last June election. That we are not concerned about. But if hon. members feel that they will be in an easier position; if they say, "Well, if you want those things which are now in force and which are operating in a manner which is generally satisfactory, to continue in operation, do not ask us to say that they should continue, but we will allow you to say so." That is a matter of indifference. What we shall ask this committee to do is to say that they shall continue or that we shall have the right to say that they shall continue because we think they are necessary, and if the committee says that we shall have the right to say that they will continue we shall not hesitate about saying so.
With respect to the other point raised, my understanding is now recorded. My colleagues will respect it. Whenever any hon. member chooses to introduce a bill to repeal any of those controls which he thinks should disappear and which we think should not yet disappear we shall facliitate as much as is in our power the taking of the opinion of this house upon it.

speechtext:
Well, I agree that the minister who was then merely the hon. member for Vancouver Centre did perhaps a better job then than he is doing now, although I am not reflecting on what he is doing now. He was a very vocal if not a very consistent member of the opposition. I suggest in all earnestness that such methods are not good policy to-day. I believe that that is the sort of thing which is bringing parliamentary institutions into disrepute, because people will no longer believe in the sincerity of parties which, when they are on the opposition side of the house act one way on a question, and when they are on the government side act another way on the same question.
I am one of the twenty-five members left of those who came here in 1930. During all the time that I have been in the house I supported every measure introduced by the government if it appealed to me as a constructive measure, regardless of the sneers I might receive from this side, and I supported the opposition when I thought it was in the right, regardless of the jeers I received from the other side. I am convinced that is the * only position a member should take to-day, because I am satisfied that the government cannot do anything in the way of good government without helping along the things that I want to do. I do not believe that the government can do anything wrong, or anything that is not in the interest of the people without adversely affecting the cause I have at heart. Therefore I repeat, if we wish to be taken as sincere people we must have the same point of view when we are on this side of the question as we have when we are on the other side of the question.
I believe that we should try to come to grips with this important issue. The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the extradition treaty and suggested that it was an important issue. I believe that this is an immensely more important piece of legislation than the extradition treaty. I do not know if there is time to give.it to a special committee, but if there were time I would certainly advocate that because if we could get the hon. member for Lake Centre into a special committee I have the idea that he
would act in a much less partisan way than he does in the house, and consequently be far more useful in dealing with a matter of this kind.
I do not want the hon. gentleman to take offence at what I am going to say. He disturbs me, because when I see him in action I have the feeling that he is a man of great ability, great application, but yet a man of- if this is the proper term-tremendous ineffectiveness. He destroys the constructive effect of what he is seemingly attempting to do. I am not objecting because he aroused the Minister of Justice, but he destroyed the effect he should have had on the Minister of Justice, if, indeed, it was his hope to make the best of this bill, a bill which we all agree is necessary. He destroyed that effectiveness by the way in which he put forward his arguments. He would shake his finger and his head in protest. The result is that no cooperation is possible.
If we are sincere it should be a fairly simple matter to deal with this bill. When we start discussing the various sections of the bill, mot being trained in the law, I feel myself at a disadvantage. I think I can understand ordinary English and what words mean, but when I hear lawyers talk I am convinced that words do not mean the same thing to me as they do to the lawyers. I realize I am not the only person affected in this way. After long observation I have come to the conclusion that there is no finality to any lawsuit except that imposed by the financial resources of the persons concerned and the number of courts to which it can be taken. When either the finances or the courts are finished then the case is at an end.
I have received a great many communications in regard to bill No. 15 as it was first introduced, but I think every one of the letters and petitions had1 to do with paragraph (g) of subsection 1 of section 3. That paragraph is out, and another part of subsection 1 of section 3 is out also. That part may not seem important to the hon. member for Lake Centre, but to me it seems important. I refer to the words, "but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms." It seems to me that rather limits the application of what the hon. member says are the similar provisions in section 2 of the new bill. I would suggest that, as the hon. member for Lake Centre knows how to do legal drafting, we take up the bill section by section, and when he comes to one he does not like let him move to delete it or amend it to conform to his ideas of what controls are wanted.
National Emergency

Then we can compare the amendment with the bill and we shall have a bettor idea as to which should be maintained.
I am convinced that we shall never produce anything constructive if we continue in the attitude we have adopted so far. So, then, I would appeal to this committee either to refer the bill to a special committee, where we shall get it out of the atmosphere of this house and away from the galleries, and where we can deal with it quietly and in an orderly fashion to-achieve a certain end. Let us get down earnestly to business, each ^adding his quota of improvement to the bill ' which we are all convinced is to some extent necessary. Mention was made of the serious days ahead. Let us not delude ourselves that the days ahead will not be serious and that we do not want or will not need legislation of this kind. In my opinion it is not so much government control that is required as elasticity in government action so that it can deal with a situation as it arises or develops. That is what is involved, rather than control; it is elasticity of administration. And that, I believe, is what we should keep in mind in dealing with this matter.

include myself, being just as foolish as hon. gentlemen who now applaud. But stripped to its nakedness, if I may use that expression, what does it mean? As the hon. member for Vancouver East so well said, we all realize that some control is still necessary in this country. No one, I am quite sure, will deny or has denied that. I think that is a simple and very fair statement to make. Occasionally one becomes a bit annoyed at someone else. Perhaps we are interrupted. I have not even heard the unanimous Minister of Veterans Affairs say in this house, "It was a dirty Tory trick'-, although I have been waiting for that remark. I have not heard that remark. I know it is coming sooner or later, because he has a copyright on that, and Hansard has been full of it for the last fifteen years. I have read it.

National Emergency
But does it not simply mean this: We say, "controls?-Yes, they are necessary." I do not wish to buy eggs at the price at which the Minister of Justice bought them a while ago, or bacon at the price at which he bought it. Those were terrific prices. That was done, I gather, because it was under an administration from this side. How would it be for all political parties in the house, from now on, to do this: Let them admit that occasionally they have been wrong. This business of parties knowing perfectly well that they were wrong twenty years ago, and trying to justify it by devious ways here and now is, to my mind, complete nonsense. The man who does not admit he is wrong is the man who will never learn anything.
My real point is this, that it seems to me that what we all seek is a measure of control to avoid inflation. None of us wants these controls to go to the extent that they will frighten investment or frighten business. I think those are simple problems upon which all of us can be agreed.
Now, then what happens? We who sit over here say that the ministers of the government who sit opposite, have a great deal of information. Tell us what you want. To what extent do you want (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e), or whatever it may be? Tell us that, and then we will support you. Mainly what we have said is that this is too broad.
I do not think ministers of the crown are going to take our birthright away from us, or anything like that, by way of order in council. No, I do not think they are. But the fact that I do not think so does not alter the principle that if this bill is passed in its present broad form, parliament has given up its authority, for whatever time you may wish, unnecessarily. It may never be used. But it is neither here nor there whether it is used or not. I make this appeal: I know the people the minister has who can draw statutes. I think Mr. Varcoe is one of the ablest men in law I know, here or anywhere else. I know that he, in conjunction with the able people they have over there can say, "We are bringing down this bill. We will control prices there, and wages and exchange"-and the like. They may do that, for whatever time they say. Then surely all of those to my right and to my left and in front of me can all fall in line, because we believe in the same thing.
What are we doing? We seem to be quarreling about things which perhaps are not of major importance. We are getting off into the by-ways. But the fact remains that 47696-190
this bill should not be permitted to assume this authority, except without the greatest struggle that we over here can possibly put up.

I wish to add a word to what has been said by the hon. member for Calgary West. I had not intended to speak either, and perhaps the reason I am speaking is that I felt the minister had scolded us like rather naughty boys-though one never know3 just how much of what a trained lawyer says he really means, and how much he just says because he is a very good counsel, and is acting for his client.
But I wish to say this, that the minister at some length, and I must say with a considerable degree of warmth, argued that we were being unreasonable and uncooperative.
I am not going to waste the time of the committee by saying that we consider that it is hon. members opposite who are being uncooperative. But I wish to say this-and this is chiefly a repetition of what my colleague to my right has said-that we have no reason to doubt that a great many people throughout this country are greatly exercised about the powers conferred by this bill. One might often be mistaken about public opinion. One may get letters from people whose views are all cockeyed. But it must be clear that there is endorsation of our view. Unless reports are all wrong, when the provincial premiers were here, if we can believe reports, which appear to be credible, there was extraordinary unanimity among them-and let me add that they were not all of our stripe of political opinion- that this bill did need revision.
We then hoped that it was then going to get revision. Quite frankly I hoped that it would, and that it was going to meet the situation. But I am bound to say that as I listened to the hon. member for Lake Centre this evening, and as I read the extremely wide provisions of paragraphs (b) and (c), it seemed to me that a rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and that, as the hon. member for Lake Centre said, the new words are about as wide as the old. If I am right in thinking that there is a very strong public opinion in this matter, and if I am right in thinking that the provincial premiers had that view, then surely we are not very unreasonable in asking that some reasons be given to us.
Why, [DOT] for example, do we have all these controls over transportation by air, rail and water? Are they necessary? I must say that this evening for the very first time the minister began to take some trouble to tell us why these powers were needed. Frankly I think that in that respect he has made only a

National Emergency

beginning. I was very much unconvinced by what he said about the railroads. I would need more persuasion that it needs this control to persuade the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do what every citizen of this country wants to have done, namely, to have these priorities given to the soldiers. Let me repeat that that seemed to me most unconvincing.
I do not wish the minister to feel that we are being unreasonable. I wish him to feel that we want to cooperate. Whatever may have been the opinion two months ago, I say that, despite the fact that hon. members opposite smiled when the hon. member for Lake Centre said he was willing to cooperate, no one should doubt our desire to cooperate. Unless we are unwilling to believe that the people of Canada are not sincere in their apprehensions, then I suggest that the hon. member for Lake Centre was not unreasonable when he asked that we should have a fuller explanation from the Minister of Justice. I say to him that he should go on and finish the job, because as these words appear in the bill they go away beyond what we think is needed.
The minister referred to a speech which had been made by the leader of the opposition. I wished afterwards that he had gone on to deal with that speech. However, he was so attracted, as was the Minister of Agriculture last night, toward dealing with the speech of the hon. member for Stanstead, because it happened to contain some praise of the Liberal party-we are generous people-and I do not mean the present Liberal party-that he failed to do so. But it seems to me that we would have spent our time more profitably if the minister had-dealt with the definite points upon which the leader of the opposition agreed we needed control. He might have got an advance copy of the speech, as the Minister of Agriculture did last night in respect of the speech delivered by the hon. member for Stanstead. Had he done that, he would have known exactly what was in it.
I am really endorsing what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. It seems to me that if we start in that way; if the minister would take those controls to which the leader of the opposition agreed, and if he would draft the bill, starting from that point, we- might _find agreement before we knew where we were.

I am not given to explaining, much less to complaining. I should, however, like to tell hon. members opposite, when they pound their desks-and I am relying upon what I read in the press in Toronto this morning

and cheer the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and of my Hibernian friend the hon. member for Vancouver East, that this bill is right up their alley. It is a bill which enacts the very legislation that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and those who share his views would enact in permanency, did the people of this country in their wisdom ever call those hon. members to office.
So, when hon. members opposite express approval of the remarks of these hon. gentlemen, I would ask them to recall that there is a difference between the principles of government-in so far as they have any-professed by hon. members opposite and those of the hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar ahd Vancouver East.
I should like to draw this to the attention of the Minister of Justice. He said, as I came into the chamber a few moments ago, that the administration of the controls and the enactment of bill No. 15 were in conformity with the wishes of the great majority of the Canadian people and would have the approval of the great majority of the Canadian people. I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that statements of that kind show just how remote the government is from popular sentiment in this country, and if they have any doubt about it I suggest that they refer this matter to a committee and let the people of Canada come before that committee and tell them what they think of controls. If they do that and can convince themselves after they have heard what the people of Canada do think of these regulations and how they long to be freed from them, there will be no further opposition from at least one member of this house.
I should like to know where all these bedtime stories come from, stories of the terrible perils and the dire penalties and severe trials that await the Canadian people if the federal cabinet do not continue these controls. It would be of interest to know the source of these stories, to know their origin. We were given the story by h'on. gentlemen opposite, and I do not question their good faith, but I submit that they are too busy with their duties of office to be in very close touch with the people at large, and I suggest to them that if they will take the time to inquire, they will find out that every little person and every big person in Canada, every housewife, every grocer, every merchant, every mechanic,

National Emergency
every workingman are seeking liberation from the intolerable scourge of control that has been upon us for so long a time.
The hon. member for Vancouver East entered into a homily, as did the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, about the iniquities of the Conservative party in days gone past, but I would draw this to the attention of the committee that, whatever may have been the controls that were exercised by that party, it was during the') period of emergency, and when the period of emergency was over the cabinet control ceased. That is what I ask, and nothing more.

When I spoke on this bill when it was before the house in its original form I voiced three objections, two of which have been cured by this amendment, and the third objection I think has been pretty well met in subsection 3 of section 2, but there is one passage on which I entertain some doubts and of which I should like an explanation from the minister. It is this phraseology:
If either the Senate or House of Commons within the period of twenty-eight days . . . resolves that it be annulled . . .
I think the word "parliament" should be substituted for either house. A resolution to annul an order in council sucR as these would be in the line of legislation, and according to our constitution legislation can only be passed by parliament, which includes the Senate and the House of Commons.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This clause is taken almost verbatim from the act that was passed by the parliament of the Ignited Kingdom.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Their act says "parliament".
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, either house of parliament. I will send a copy of the act over to my hon. friend and he will find that section 4 reads, starting at line 31 on page 3:
. . . and every order in council made under this act. shall be laid before parliament as soon as may be after it is made; and if either house of parliament, within the period of forty days beginning with the day on which any such order in council, order or instrument is laid before it, resolves that it be annulled, it shall cease to have effect, . .
The reason it was expressed in this form, that if either house of parliament resolves that it be annulled it shall cease to have effect, is not because the resolution is regarded as legislation, but because the order in council is regarded as legislation on the assumption that the crown had the consent of both houses of parliament. If either house within the period of twenty-eight days from the time the 47696-190i
order in council is placed before it expresses itself by resolution to the contrary, then the order ceases to have legislative effect.

The Minister of Justice said that it was an assumption of the governor in council when an order in council was passed that both houses would approve the order, which is legislation. It may be answered that if both houses adopt bill No. 15, we are surrendering to the government our legislative powers in given matters and that therefore there is no need of this assumption by the governor in council. As an hon. member on the other, side of the house said, when parliament wants to withdraw or to annul an order in council, it is new legislation, and I submit very respectfully that, under our constitution it should be by both houses.
There is another argument, which arises from a practical point of view. Decontrol will be a very difficult thing. Why take the risk that one or both houses would study the matter rapidly, and in supposedly taking off the price ceiling on one commodity, risk a crumbling of the whole economy of control? I think it will be quite easy to add, after the word "annulled" in the fifth line of page 3, the following words, "and the said resolution is concurred in by the other chamber, after formal notification by the initiating chamber," then "it shall cease to have effect." The question I should like to ask is confirmed particularly to paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 2, and has to do first of all with the demobilization of the armed forces. Can the minister explain what he has in mind, in view of the fact that extensive powers have already been given to the government up to the end of March, 1946, by bill No. 172, at which time I presume this house will again be in session?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: But at which time the whole of the Canadian troops will not have been demobilized. It is felt that the orders made in that behalf should be such that they can continue to operate as long as there are men being demobilized. These appropriation bills have to deal with the fiscal year; there are a great many things which are done and which have been done, and possibly there may be some more which will have to be done, dealing with the maintenance of the armed forces during the occupation of enemy territory and also with demobilization. The regulations dealing with demobilization are continuing regulations. I think we can probably bring most of them, if not all of them, under the terms of the Militia Act; but during the war we had one act that we could always fall back on. If the Department of Justice were asked if such-and-such an order in council could be made and there was nothing else turned up to justify it there was always the War Measures Act that permitted its being done. I think most of what would be done, for demobilization purposes could be enacted under the Militia Act, but there may be something that has not been foreseen under the Militia Act. Of course under the War Measures Act things were done to relieve suffering in foreign countries. Military relief was provided as part of the military operations, and that was paid for from money appropriated under the war appropriation and under powers conferred by the war appropriation and the War Measures Act. But this is something looking to the possibility of having to do these things during this future period. Of course it does not authorize the governor in council to use any money not appropriated for such purposes or not appropriated in a way that is broad enough to include such purposes. This is the clause that would be relied upon for the purpose of rationing meat or any other rationing that might be imposed to -make greater supplies available for relief purposes. The terms in which it is drawn were taken verbatim from the British bill. The way in which it came about was exactly that. The question was put, where is there here anything that would authorize the rationing of supplies in Canada for the purpose of making greater quantities available for the relief of distress elsewhere? and we were somewhat puzzled as to where we would find the appropriate clause in the bill. We had before us the British act, and we copied that clause word for word.

speechtext:
The government has assured us that it is not seeking any powers it does not absolutely require, but I cannot escape a feeling of anxiety about the powers it now has. It has powers under two separate acts until March 31, 1946. If hon. gentlemen opposite will read the provisions of the war expenditures appropriation measure they will find that in section 5 the government has practically all the powers for which it asks under the present bill, until March 31, 1946. Since there is provision in bill No. 15 for the tabling of orders in council passed under it, would the minister be prepared to give any assurance that orders in council passed concerning the powers given under this bill will be passed under this bill, so that they will be tabled in the house, rather than under the other act, in order that we may not know what is going on?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think I can give the hon. member any assurance in that regard. The powers in the appropriation act are for the expenditure of the money that has been provided by that act, and I could not give any assurance that when an order in council is passed for the purpose of dealing with some of the money voted in that measure a reference will be made to this bill for the purpose of bringing it before the house. There has to be an accounting of the money that has been expended under the other act; and if this measure was not before the house at all the terms of the other legislation would still be there. If it was felt proper to pass the other bill in the form in which it has been passed I do not think a suggestion should be made at this time that we are going to get powers here but we are going to try to avoid tabling what we do under those powers. We will,

so long as I have anything to say about the matter, try to avoid using these emergency powers-because I do not like them. I think that in the Department of Justice we should endeavour to have done whatever is being done under the permanent legislation. That will be the attempt, so long as I am in that department. When we are consulted, we will try to find a legal way under the permanent legislation of doing what is required.
But of course when it will come to legislating or making new legislation by orders in council we may have to use these provisions. There are some other statutes under which the governor in council is given power to legislate, and the war appropriation measure was a statute of that kind. But it contemplates regulations only to deal with the money that is provided by the statute, and those regulations must not go beyond what is to be paid for out of money provided by statute. It cannot be used mainly for the purpose of making the regulations. The regulation must be incidental to the expenditure of the money.

What I now ask is this: Will the minister carry out that undertaking and exercise the powers under the present measure, under which he has said he will table orders in council so that we may know what is being done, rather than under the previous measure to which we objected? maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: BILL TO CONFER CERTAIN POWERS UPON THE GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish for only two or three minutes to voice my opposition to this bill. It is the very same bill in a new form as was proposed before, giving vast powers to the governor in council. As hon. members know, under the original War Measures Act and bill No. 15 the courts of this countrythe high courts, the county courts, and the magistrates' courts-have before them cases to decide and give decisions based on the powers herein of the governor in council.
After the dominion-provincial conference which met last week some of those persons who spoke to the newspapers described bill No. 15 as the Donald Gordon plan. This new plan gives the governor in council powers to look after the maintenance of the armed forces of Canada, all trade and commerce and so on. In fact, it is the identical style of bill with the identical powers.
They have abolished these controls in Australia, and the President of the United States has practically eliminated them in that great country. Let me point out that under section 2 there is no doubt that people will be summonsed to court-police courts and other courts of competent jurisdiction-to answer to the same irksome control offences. Is this Liberalism as we have it in this country to-day? Is this what you call Liberalism? -control over the lives of every person, control over every man, woman and child in Canada, and the abolition of statutes which for 200 years have protected the liberty of the subject and of all reference to the law courts who have no control? Everything in the bill is removed from the controls of those courts. They would not stand for this in the United States. Why, we have a regular small standing army of officials in that country. The government knows something of what is going on. That standing army would reach from here to Lansdowne park. The expeditionary force we have over there should learn something of what is being done in that country to abolish all controls. But they have learned nothing.
Over there they have abolished controls. Under section 2 of this bill the small and large businessman would be put out of business. The difference between the new bill and the old one is the difference between Tweedledum and Tweedledee. That is the only difference between these two plans.
Under paragraph (a) the governor in council has power to provide for and maintain the armed forces of Canada during the occupation of enemy territory; it has power to facilitate the readjustment of industry, and also other powers. Small and large business, and every manufacturer in the country have been asking for the removal of these irksome controls. How does the government expect war-time economies to be turned into peace-time economies of large and small business when we have these irksome controls placed upon individuals?
Questions

The people whom we have been giving credit < for the formulation of this new plan will be glad to be free of it, when they see how unpopular it is throughout the country. I know something of the way in which these irksome controls have operated during the war years and the effect they have had on business generally.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
